CHANGELOG.md.text:
# Changelog

All notable changes to benchbloom are documented here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and the project aims
to adhere to Semantic Versioning.

## [Unreleased]

### Changed
- Pinned the lint toolchain in `requirements-dev.txt`; dependabot now watches it.
- Recorded the dev-tooling pin and the dependency update path in the
  contributing guide.

### Fixed
- `cpp/bloomdex.cpp` now includes `<unordered_map>`; the engine did not
  compile on a clean checkout because `std::unordered_multimap` was used
  without its header.

## [0.1.0] - 2026-09-01

### Added
- Pure-stdlib Python orchestrator (`benchbloom`) with `normalize`, `scan`,
  `index`, and `report` subcommands.
- JSONL / text ingestion with tolerant parsing and NFKC-based normalization.
- Exact n-gram shingling with Jaccard and containment leakage metrics.
- C++17 engine `bloomdex` implementing token-shingle MinHash signatures and
  candidate overlap scoring (`sign`, `match`, `self`).
- Direct `g++`/`clang++` build via `Makefile` and `cpp/build.sh` (no CMake).
- Worked examples: reference/subject corpora and an end-to-end walkthrough.
- CI workflow compiling the C++ engine and syntax-checking the Python package.

### Notes
- MinHash overlap is an estimate; use `scan` for exact verification on small
  corpora. Estimator variance narrows as `--k` increases.

# Contributing

Thanks for looking. A few things that make a change easy to take:

1. Open an issue first for anything larger than a bug fix, so we agree on the shape.
2. Keep the change focused - one behaviour per pull request.
3. Run the checks before opening the PR:
- `make` (builds `cpp/bloomdex`)
- `python -m benchbloom scan --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl --subject examples/training.jsonl`
4. Add a test for the behaviour you changed.
5. Match the surrounding style; the codebase is deliberately small and flat.
6. Dev tooling is pinned in `requirements-dev.txt`; bump pins deliberately.

README.md.text:
# 🌸 benchbloom **A forensic herbarium for benchmark contamination.** *Press your benchmark between glass, dust it for spores, and read the pollen count where a training corpus brushed against it.* ![pipeline](docs/assets/pipeline.svg)
--- ## Field notes before you begin Contamination is quiet. A benchmark item does not announce that it has already been seen during training — it simply germinates, unnoticed, until the day your model scores suspiciously well and you cannot say why. benchbloom is a small, patient instrument for finding those germinated seeds. It treats every corpus like a pressed plant specimen: flatten it, catalogue its parts, and compare the spore prints of two specimens to see whether one grew from the other. There are two instruments on this bench, and they are meant to be used together: - **`benchbloom`** — a pure-Python-standard-library orchestrator. It is the botanist: it collects specimens (JSONL or text), presses and dries them (normalization), and can either read the exact venation of every leaf itself (n-gram / Jaccard) or hand the specimens to the microscope for a faster, approximate reading. - **`bloomdex`** — a C++17 microscope. It grinds each specimen into token shingles, takes a MinHash spore print, and reports where two prints overlap. It reads at high throughput and streams so that a specimen larger than memory still fits on the slide. No external libraries. No CMake. No test suite shipped (by design — this release is a foundation). Just a botanist, a microscope, and a drawer of honest labels. --- ## Why a botanical metaphor, and why it is not just decoration The metaphor earns its keep because contamination detection genuinely behaves like comparing biological specimens: | Botany | benchbloom | | --- | --- | | Pressing & drying a specimen | Normalization: NFKC fold, lowercase, collapse whitespace, drop punctuation | | A leaf's venation pattern | The set of token n-gram *shingles* of a record | | Two leaves sharing venation | High **Jaccard** / **containment** between shingle sets | | A spore print on paper | A **MinHash signature**: K min-hashes standing in for the whole set | | Matching spore prints under glass | Estimated Jaccard = fraction of matching min-positions | | A short cutting embedded in a larger plant | **Containment**: a benchmark item copied inside a long training doc | Containment is the metaphor that matters most. Real leakage rarely looks like two identical documents. It looks like one small benchmark question pressed flat inside a sprawling web-scraped paragraph. Jaccard punishes that size mismatch; containment does not. benchbloom triggers on containment by default and reports Jaccard alongside it, so you can see both the strict and the sensitive reading. --- ## The bench layout ``` benchbloom/ ├── benchbloom/ # the botanist (pure stdlib Python) │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── __main__.py # python -m benchbloom │ ├── cli.py # normalize | scan | index | report │ ├── ingest.py # JSONL/text loaders + normalization │ ├── metrics.py # exact n-gram shingling, Jaccard, containment │ └── engine.py # bridge to the C++ microscope ├── cpp/ # the microscope (C++17, no deps) │ ├── bloomdex.cpp # sign | match | self │ └── build.sh # direct clang++/g++ build ├── examples/ # two pressed specimens + a walkthrough │ ├── benchmark.jsonl │ ├── training.jsonl │ └── README.md ├── docs/assets/ # two animated SVG plates │ ├── pipeline.svg │ └── lattice.svg ├── .github/workflows/ci.yml # compile C++, syntax-check Python, smoke test ├── Makefile # make -> cpp/bloomdex ├── pyproject.toml ├── CHANGELOG.md · ROADMAP.md · LICENSE ``` ![lattice](docs/assets/lattice.svg) --- ## Preparing the bench (build the microscope) The Python botanist needs nothing but a standard Python 3.8+ interpreter. The C++ microscope must be ground from its single translation unit. Pick either door — both call the compiler directly, no CMake in sight. ```bash # Door 1: Makefile make # produces cpp/bloomdex # Door 2: the build script (auto-detects clang++ or g++) bash cpp/build.sh # Door 3: by hand, if you enjoy the sound of it g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic cpp/bloomdex.cpp -o cpp/bloomdex ``` On Windows with MinGW the same one-liner works; the resulting binary is `cpp/bloomdex.exe`, and the Python bridge already knows to look for the `.exe` suffix. If a build complains about `std::unordered_multimap`, it predates the `` include fix - pull latest and rebuild. --- ## A first pressing (the exact reading) You do not need the microscope to get an exact answer on modest specimens. The botanist can read venation directly: ```bash python -m benchbloom scan \ --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \ --subject examples/training.jsonl \ --field text --ngram 4 --threshold 0.3 ``` This prints a JSON report to stdout and a one-line **verdict** to stderr. In the shipped example, benchmark items `b1`, `b2`, and `b4` were quietly transplanted into the training set, and the scan will flag them with high containment. Items `b3` (a fact about prime numbers) and `b5` (an invented city) never took root and stay clean. The report looks like this: ```json { "summary": { "ref_items": 5, "flagged_pairs": 3, "contaminated_ref_items": 3, "contamination_rate": 0.6, "peak_overlap": 1.0 }, "pairs": [ { "ref_id": "b1", "subject_id": "t5", "jaccard": 0.72, "containment": 1.0 }, ... ] } ``` The **verdict** grades the contamination rate on a simple herbarium scale: - `CLEAN` — nothing germinated above threshold. - `TRACE` — an isolated seedling; inspect the flagged pairs by hand. - `ELEVATED` — meaningful contamination; the benchmark is compromised in part. - `HEAVY` — the specimen is overgrown; treat scores from it with suspicion. --- ## The microscope reading (MinHash at scale) Exact shingling is O(unique-shingles) in memory and quadratic in specimens. When the corpus grows past comfort, hand it to the microscope. The `index` subcommand orchestrates the whole assay: press both specimens, take their spore prints, and overlay the prints. ```bash python -m benchbloom index \ --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \ --subject examples/training.jsonl \ --field text --k 128 --ngram 4 --threshold 0.4 \ --out match.tsv python -m benchbloom report match.tsv ``` Under the hood the botanist: 1. Loads and normalizes both corpora, writing one dried record per line. 2. Calls `bloomdex sign` on each to produce a signature file — `K` 64-bit min-hashes per record, drawn from `K` universal hash seeds over the record's shingle set. 3. Calls `bloomdex match` to compare every reference print against every subject print, emitting a TSV of pairs whose *estimated* Jaccard clears the threshold. The estimate is honest but approximate. The variance of a MinHash Jaccard estimate shrinks roughly with `1/√K`, so `--k 128` gives you a standard error near 0.09 and `--k 512` roughly halves it. When in doubt, confirm a flagged pair with the exact `scan`. The microscope finds candidates; the botanist confirms the diagnosis. ### Reading a spore print by hand You can drive the microscope directly, without the botanist, if you already have normalized text (one record per line): ```bash cpp/bloomdex sign --input ref.norm.txt --out ref.sig --k 256 --ngram 5 cpp/bloomdex sign --input sub.norm.txt --out sub.sig --k 256 --ngram 5 cpp/bloomdex match --ref ref.sig --subject sub.sig --out match.tsv --threshold 0.5 # find near-duplicates *within* a single corpus (deduplication) cpp/bloomdex self --input sub.sig --out dups.tsv --threshold 0.8 ``` A signature line is deliberately plain text so you can inspect it with any tool: ``` r423188823... 199... 40.. (K space-separated 64-bit min-hashes) ``` --- ## How the spore print is actually taken For the curious, here is the honest mechanism, no hand-waving: - **Shingles.** Each normalized record is split into tokens; every window of `ngram` consecutive tokens is joined with a unit-separator byte (`0x1f`) to form one shingle. The separator prevents `["a","bc"]` and `["ab","c"]` from colliding into the same string. - **Base hash.** Each shingle is hashed with 64-bit FNV-1a into a base value. - **Permutations.** `K` universal hash functions of the form `(a·x + b) mod (2⁶¹−1)` permute that base value. The coefficients `a, b` come from a `splitmix64` stream seeded deterministically, so two runs on two machines produce identical prints — a property you want in forensics. - **Min selection.** For each of the `K` functions we keep the minimum permuted value across all shingles. That vector of `K` minima is the signature. - **Estimate.** The estimated Jaccard between two records is simply the fraction of the `K` positions where their minima agree — the classic MinHash identity. Short records (fewer tokens than `ngram`) degrade gracefully: the whole record becomes a single shingle rather than vanishing from the assay. --- ## Command reference ### `benchbloom normalize` Press and dry a corpus into one normalized record per line — the format the microscope consumes. ```bash python -m benchbloom normalize input.jsonl --out dried.txt --field text --field title ``` ### `benchbloom scan` Exact n-gram / Jaccard / containment report, Python only. Flags on containment by default; pass `--jaccard-only` to trigger on Jaccard instead. `--top N` keeps only the N strongest pairs in the JSON body. ### `benchbloom index` Full orchestration through the C++ engine. `--k` sets signature width, `--ngram` the shingle size, `--threshold` the estimated-Jaccard cutoff, `--engine` an explicit path to the binary, and `--workdir` a place to keep intermediates. ### `benchbloom report` Render a saved `match.tsv` into a human summary with the strongest overlaps listed first. ### `bloomdex sign | match | self` The microscope's three lenses: build signatures, compare two signature sets, and find near-duplicates within one set. Run `bloomdex --help` for the exact flags. --- ## Interpreting results without fooling yourself A few honest cautions from the field log: - **Threshold is a dial, not a truth.** A high threshold misses paraphrased leakage; a low one drowns you in coincidental n-gram overlap. Sweep it. - **Containment finds the small-in-large case.** If your benchmark items are short and your training docs are long, prefer the default containment trigger. - **MinHash is a screen, not a verdict.** Treat every flagged pair as a candidate and confirm the important ones with the exact `scan`. - **Normalization changes the answer.** Stripping punctuation merges more items; keeping it (`--keep-punct`) is stricter. Pick one and stay consistent across a study. - **This tool detects textual overlap.** Semantic contamination — the same question rephrased entirely — is out of scope here and always will be for an n-gram instrument. Do not claim more than the spore print shows. --- ## What is honestly finished, and what is not This release is a **foundation**, and the [ROADMAP](ROADMAP.md) says so plainly. Four foundation milestones are implemented and verified: ingestion & normalization, exact leakage metrics, the C++17 MinHash engine, and the Python↔C++ orchestration. Everything past that — LSH banding, binary signature formats, multi-field attribution, HTML reports, threaded signing — is planned, not built. There is no benchmark suite, so no throughput number is claimed as fact; "high-throughput" describes the streaming design, not a measured figure. There are, deliberately, **no unit tests** in this release. The CI instead compiles the C++ engine, syntax-checks every Python module, and runs the example assay end to end as a smoke test. Tests are welcome future work. --- ## License Released under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Press what you like, share the prints freely.
Grown on a quiet bench, one spore print at a time. 🌱

ROADMAP.md.text:
# Roadmap

benchbloom follows a foundation-first plan. The milestones below marked done
are the ones actually implemented and verified in this repository. Everything
under "Planned" is aspirational and not yet built.

## Foundation (verified in this release)

- [x] **M1 — Ingestion & normalization.** JSONL/text loaders with tolerant
  parsing and deterministic NFKC + whitespace/punctuation normalization.
  Implemented in `benchbloom/ingest.py`.
- [x] **M2 — Exact leakage metrics.** Token n-gram shingling with Jaccard and
  containment scoring and a report summarizer. Implemented in
  `benchbloom/metrics.py`.
- [x] **M3 — C++17 MinHash engine.** `bloomdex` builds min-hash signatures over
  token shingles and scores candidate overlap; compiles cleanly with `g++`
  `-std=c++17`. Implemented in `cpp/bloomdex.cpp`.
- [x] **M4 — Python↔C++ orchestration.** The `index` subcommand normalizes,
  signs, and matches through the engine bridge in `benchbloom/engine.py`.

## Planned (not yet implemented)

- [ ] LSH banding to prune the O(N·M) match loop toward near-linear behavior.
- [ ] Streaming signature format with a compact binary encoding.
- [ ] Multi-field weighting and per-field contamination attribution.
- [ ] HTML report export with highlighted overlapping shingles.
- [ ] Parallel signing across shards / threads in the C++ engine.

Honesty note: performance claims for the C++ engine are qualitative
("high-throughput streaming") — no formal benchmark suite ships yet, and none
is claimed here.

SECURITY.md.text:
# Security Policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please do not open a public issue for a security problem. Use GitHub's private
[security advisory](https://github.com/kMegapnbedt/BenchBloom/security/advisories/new) form, or contact a
maintainer directly if the form is unavailable to you.

Include what an attacker gains in one sentence, the version or commit you are running, the smallest
reproduction you can manage, and whether the input is attacker-controlled in your setup. You should
get an acknowledgement within a few working days and a disclosure timeline before anything is
published.

## Scope

benchbloom normalizes untrusted corpora and renders match reports. Malformed JSONL,
oversized records, path handling in `--workdir`/`--out` and TSV report parsing are in
scope; the C++ engine parses files produced by the Python front end.

benchbloom/__init__.py.text:
"""benchbloom — benchmark contamination detector (Python orchestrator).

Pure standard library. Ingests JSONL/text corpora, normalizes records, and
either computes exact n-gram/Jaccard leakage reports in Python or delegates
high-throughput MinHash signature work to the companion C++ engine `bloomdex`.
"""

__version__ = "0.1.0"

benchbloom/cli.py.text:
"""benchbloom command-line interface (pure standard library).

Subcommands
-----------
normalize   Ingest JSONL/text and emit a normalized, one-record-per-line file.
scan        Exact n-gram/Jaccard leakage report (Python only).
index       Orchestrate the C++ engine: normalize -> sign -> match.
report      Render a saved TSV match report into a human summary.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from . import __version__, engine, ingest, metrics


def _cmd_normalize(args: argparse.Namespace) -> int:
    records = ingest.load(args.input, fields=args.field, id_field=args.id_field)
    n = ingest.write_normalized(records, args.out, strip_punct=not args.keep_punct)
    print(f"normalized {n} records -> {args.out}")
    return 0


def _cmd_scan(args: argparse.Namespace) -> int:
    ref = ingest.load(args.ref, fields=args.field, id_field=args.id_field)
    sub = ingest.load(args.subject, fields=args.field, id_field=args.id_field)
    ref_norm = [(r.rid, ingest.normalize(r.text)) for r in ref]
    sub_norm = [(s.rid, ingest.normalize(s.text)) for s in sub]

    ref_idx = metrics.build_shingle_index(ref_norm, args.ngram)
    sub_idx = metrics.build_shingle_index(sub_norm, args.ngram)
    pairs = metrics.cross_leakage(ref_idx, sub_idx, threshold=args.threshold,
                                  use_containment=not args.jaccard_only)
    summary = metrics.summarize(pairs, len(ref_idx))

    report = {
        "summary": summary,
        "pairs": [vars(p) for p in pairs[: args.top]] if args.top else [vars(p) for p in pairs],
    }
    text = json.dumps(report, indent=2)
    if args.out:
        Path(args.out).write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        print(f"scan report -> {args.out}")
    else:
        print(text)
    _print_verdict(summary)
    return 0


def _cmd_index(args: argparse.Namespace) -> int:
    eng = engine.find_engine(args.engine)
    if not eng:
        print("error: bloomdex engine not found. Build it with cpp/build.sh or make.",
              file=sys.stderr)
        return 3

    workdir = Path(args.workdir) if args.workdir else Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="benchbloom_"))
    workdir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    ref = ingest.load(args.ref, fields=args.field, id_field=args.id_field)
    sub = ingest.load(args.subject, fields=args.field, id_field=args.id_field)
    ref_norm = workdir / "ref.norm.txt"
    sub_norm = workdir / "subject.norm.txt"
    ingest.write_normalized(ref, ref_norm)
    ingest.write_normalized(sub, sub_norm)

    ref_sig = workdir / "ref.sig"
    sub_sig = workdir / "subject.sig"
    print(engine.sign(eng, str(ref_norm), str(ref_sig), k=args.k, ngram=args.ngram))
    print(engine.sign(eng, str(sub_norm), str(sub_sig), k=args.k, ngram=args.ngram))

    match_out = Path(args.out) if args.out else workdir / "match.tsv"
    print(engine.match(eng, str(ref_sig), str(sub_sig), str(match_out),
                       threshold=args.threshold))
    rows = engine.parse_match_report(match_out)

    contaminated = {r.ref_id for r in rows}
    summary = {
        "ref_items": len(ref),
        "flagged_pairs": len(rows),
        "contaminated_ref_items": len(contaminated),
        "contamination_rate": round(len(contaminated) / len(ref), 4) if ref else 0.0,
        "peak_overlap": round(max((r.jaccard for r in rows), default=0.0), 4),
    }
    print(f"match report -> {match_out}")
    _print_verdict(summary)
    return 0


def _cmd_report(args: argparse.Namespace) -> int:
    rows = engine.parse_match_report(args.input)
    contaminated = {r.ref_id for r in rows}
    print(f"flagged pairs        : {len(rows)}")
    print(f"contaminated ref ids : {len(contaminated)}")
    if rows:
        top = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r.jaccard, reverse=True)[: args.top]
        print("top overlaps:")
        for r in top:
            print(f"  {r.ref_id:>10}  <->  {r.subject_id:<10}  jaccard={r.jaccard:.3f}")
    return 0


def _print_verdict(summary: dict) -> None:
    rate = summary.get("contamination_rate", 0.0)
    if rate == 0.0:
        verdict = "CLEAN — no leakage above threshold"
    elif rate < 0.05:
        verdict = "TRACE — isolated overlap, inspect flagged pairs"
    elif rate < 0.25:
        verdict = "ELEVATED — meaningful contamination present"
    else:
        verdict = "HEAVY — benchmark likely compromised"
    print(f"verdict: {verdict} (rate={rate})", file=sys.stderr)


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="benchbloom",
                                description="benchmark contamination detector")
    p.add_argument("--version", action="version", version=f"benchbloom {__version__}")
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)

    def add_common(sp):
        sp.add_argument("--field", action="append", help="JSON text field(s) to read")
        sp.add_argument("--id-field", help="JSON field to use as record id")
        sp.add_argument("--ngram", type=int, default=5, help="token n-gram size")

    pn = sub.add_parser("normalize", help="ingest and normalize a corpus")
    pn.add_argument("input")
    pn.add_argument("--out", required=True)
    pn.add_argument("--field", action="append")
    pn.add_argument("--id-field")
    pn.add_argument("--keep-punct", action="store_true")
    pn.set_defaults(func=_cmd_normalize)

    ps = sub.add_parser("scan", help="exact Python n-gram/Jaccard leakage report")
    ps.add_argument("--ref", required=True)
    ps.add_argument("--subject", required=True)
    ps.add_argument("--out")
    ps.add_argument("--threshold", type=float, default=0.3)
    ps.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=0)
    ps.add_argument("--jaccard-only", action="store_true")
    add_common(ps)
    ps.set_defaults(func=_cmd_scan)

    pi = sub.add_parser("index", help="orchestrate the C++ MinHash engine")
    pi.add_argument("--ref", required=True)
    pi.add_argument("--subject", required=True)
    pi.add_argument("--out")
    pi.add_argument("--engine", help="path to bloomdex binary")
    pi.add_argument("--workdir")
    pi.add_argument("--k", type=int, default=128)
    pi.add_argument("--threshold", type=float, default=0.5)
    add_common(pi)
    pi.set_defaults(func=_cmd_index)

    pr = sub.add_parser("report", help="summarize a saved TSV match report")
    pr.add_argument("input")
    pr.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=10)
    pr.set_defaults(func=_cmd_report)

    return p


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    parser = build_parser()
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    return args.func(args)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

"""Ingestion and normalization for benchbloom.

Reads JSONL or plain-text corpora into a uniform list of records, then applies
deterministic text normalization so that leakage comparisons are robust to
whitespace, casing, and punctuation noise.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
import unicodedata
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Iterable, Iterator, List

_WS_RE = re.compile(r"\s+")
_NONALNUM_RE = re.compile(r"[^0-9a-z ]+")


@dataclass
class Record:
    """A single corpus item after ingestion."""

    rid: str
    text: str
    meta: dict = field(default_factory=dict)


def normalize(text: str, *, strip_punct: bool = True) -> str:
    """Lowercase, NFKC-fold, collapse whitespace; optionally drop punctuation.

    The output is stable and idempotent, which matters for reproducible
    n-gram/Jaccard reports.
    """
    if not text:
        return ""
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text)
    text = text.lower()
    if strip_punct:
        text = _NONALNUM_RE.sub(" ", text)
    text = _WS_RE.sub(" ", text).strip()
    return text


def _extract_text(obj: dict, fields: List[str]) -> str:
    """Pull and concatenate the configured text fields from a JSON object."""
    parts: List[str] = []
    for f in fields:
        val = obj.get(f)
        if isinstance(val, str):
            parts.append(val)
        elif isinstance(val, (list, tuple)):
            parts.extend(str(v) for v in val if isinstance(v, (str, int, float)))
    return " ".join(parts)


def read_jsonl(path: Path, fields: List[str], id_field: str | None = None) -> Iterator[Record]:
    """Stream a JSONL file into Records, skipping malformed lines gracefully."""
    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for i, line in enumerate(fh):
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            try:
                obj = json.loads(line)
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                # Tolerate the occasional broken line rather than aborting a scan.
                continue
            if not isinstance(obj, dict):
                obj = {"text": str(obj)}
            text = _extract_text(obj, fields) if fields else str(obj.get("text", ""))
            rid = str(obj.get(id_field, f"j{i}")) if id_field else f"j{i}"
            yield Record(rid=rid, text=text, meta={k: obj[k] for k in obj if k not in fields})


def read_text(path: Path) -> Iterator[Record]:
    """Stream a plain-text file: one record per non-empty line."""
    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for i, line in enumerate(fh):
            line = line.rstrip("\n")
            if line.strip():
                yield Record(rid=f"t{i}", text=line, meta={})


def load(path: str | Path, *, fields: Iterable[str] | None = None,
         id_field: str | None = None) -> List[Record]:
    """Load a corpus from JSONL (.jsonl/.json) or text, auto-detected by suffix."""
    p = Path(path)
    if not p.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"corpus not found: {p}")
    field_list = list(fields) if fields else ["text"]
    if p.suffix.lower() in {".jsonl", ".json", ".ndjson"}:
        return list(read_jsonl(p, field_list, id_field))
    return list(read_text(p))


def write_normalized(records: Iterable[Record], out_path: str | Path,
                     *, strip_punct: bool = True) -> int:
    """Write one normalized record per line; returns the count written.

    This is the hand-off format consumed by the C++ `bloomdex sign` command.
    """
    out = Path(out_path)
    out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    n = 0
    with out.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for rec in records:
            norm = normalize(rec.text, strip_punct=strip_punct)
            fh.write(norm + "\n")
            n += 1
    return n

set -euo pipefail

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"

    if command -v clang++ >/dev/null 2>&1; then CXX=clang++
    elif command -v g++ >/dev/null 2>&1; then CXX=g++
    else echo "error: no clang++ or g++ found on PATH" >&2; exit 1
    fi
fi

echo "building bloomdex with $CXX ($FLAGS)"
"$CXX" $FLAGS "$SRC" -o "$OUT"
echo "built: $OUT"

examples/README.md.text:
# Examples

Two tiny corpora ship here so you can watch benchbloom flag contamination:

- `benchmark.jsonl` — 5 held-out benchmark items (the "reference").
- `training.jsonl` — 6 training documents (the "subject"). Items `t1`, `t2`,
  and `t5` deliberately paraphrase or copy benchmark items `b2`, `b4`, and `b1`.

## Exact Python scan (no compiler needed)

```bash
python -m benchbloom scan \
  --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \
  --subject examples/training.jsonl \
  --field text --ngram 4 --threshold 0.3
```

Pins live in `requirements-dev.txt`; the examples assume the
stock interpreter, no packages required.

You should see `b1`, `b2`, and `b4` flagged with high containment, and a
`verdict:` line printed to stderr.

## MinHash engine path (requires the C++ build)

```bash
# 1) build the engine
make            # or: bash cpp/build.sh

# 2) orchestrate normalize -> sign -> match through bloomdex
python -m benchbloom index \
  --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \
  --subject examples/training.jsonl \
  --field text --k 128 --ngram 4 --threshold 0.4 \
  --out match.tsv

# 3) render the report
python -m benchbloom report match.tsv
```

The estimated Jaccard from MinHash will track (not exactly equal) the exact
scan; raise `--k` to tighten the estimate.

# Changelog

All notable changes to benchbloom are documented here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and the project aims
to adhere to Semantic Versioning.

## [Unreleased]

### Changed
- Pinned the lint toolchain in `requirements-dev.txt`; dependabot now watches it.
- Recorded the dev-tooling pin and the dependency update path in the
  contributing guide.

### Fixed
- `cpp/bloomdex.cpp` now includes `<unordered_map>`; the engine did not
  compile on a clean checkout because `std::unordered_multimap` was used
  without its header.

## [0.1.0] - 2026-09-01

### Added
- Pure-stdlib Python orchestrator (`benchbloom`) with `normalize`, `scan`,
  `index`, and `report` subcommands.
- JSONL / text ingestion with tolerant parsing and NFKC-based normalization.
- Exact n-gram shingling with Jaccard and containment leakage metrics.
- C++17 engine `bloomdex` implementing token-shingle MinHash signatures and
  candidate overlap scoring (`sign`, `match`, `self`).
- Direct `g++`/`clang++` build via `Makefile` and `cpp/build.sh` (no CMake).
- Worked examples: reference/subject corpora and an end-to-end walkthrough.
- CI workflow compiling the C++ engine and syntax-checking the Python package.

### Notes
- MinHash overlap is an estimate; use `scan` for exact verification on small
  corpora. Estimator variance narrows as `--k` increases.

README.md.text:
# 🌸 benchbloom **A forensic herbarium for benchmark contamination.** *Press your benchmark between glass, dust it for spores, and read the pollen count where a training corpus brushed against it.* ![pipeline](docs/assets/pipeline.svg)
--- ## Field notes before you begin Contamination is quiet. A benchmark item does not announce that it has already been seen during training — it simply germinates, unnoticed, until the day your model scores suspiciously well and you cannot say why. benchbloom is a small, patient instrument for finding those germinated seeds. It treats every corpus like a pressed plant specimen: flatten it, catalogue its parts, and compare the spore prints of two specimens to see whether one grew from the other. There are two instruments on this bench, and they are meant to be used together: - **`benchbloom`** — a pure-Python-standard-library orchestrator. It is the botanist: it collects specimens (JSONL or text), presses and dries them (normalization), and can either read the exact venation of every leaf itself (n-gram / Jaccard) or hand the specimens to the microscope for a faster, approximate reading. - **`bloomdex`** — a C++17 microscope. It grinds each specimen into token shingles, takes a MinHash spore print, and reports where two prints overlap. It reads at high throughput and streams so that a specimen larger than memory still fits on the slide. No external libraries. No CMake. No test suite shipped (by design — this release is a foundation). Just a botanist, a microscope, and a drawer of honest labels. --- ## Why a botanical metaphor, and why it is not just decoration The metaphor earns its keep because contamination detection genuinely behaves like comparing biological specimens: | Botany | benchbloom | | --- | --- | | Pressing & drying a specimen | Normalization: NFKC fold, lowercase, collapse whitespace, drop punctuation | | A leaf's venation pattern | The set of token n-gram *shingles* of a record | | Two leaves sharing venation | High **Jaccard** / **containment** between shingle sets | | A spore print on paper | A **MinHash signature**: K min-hashes standing in for the whole set | | Matching spore prints under glass | Estimated Jaccard = fraction of matching min-positions | | A short cutting embedded in a larger plant | **Containment**: a benchmark item copied inside a long training doc | Containment is the metaphor that matters most. Real leakage rarely looks like two identical documents. It looks like one small benchmark question pressed flat inside a sprawling web-scraped paragraph. Jaccard punishes that size mismatch; containment does not. benchbloom triggers on containment by default and reports Jaccard alongside it, so you can see both the strict and the sensitive reading. --- ## The bench layout ``` benchbloom/ ├── benchbloom/ # the botanist (pure stdlib Python) │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── __main__.py # python -m benchbloom │ ├── cli.py # normalize | scan | index | report │ ├── ingest.py # JSONL/text loaders + normalization │ ├── metrics.py # exact n-gram shingling, Jaccard, containment │ └── engine.py # bridge to the C++ microscope ├── cpp/ # the microscope (C++17, no deps) │ ├── bloomdex.cpp # sign | match | self │ └── build.sh # direct clang++/g++ build ├── examples/ # two pressed specimens + a walkthrough │ ├── benchmark.jsonl │ ├── training.jsonl │ └── README.md ├── docs/assets/ # two animated SVG plates │ ├── pipeline.svg │ └── lattice.svg ├── .github/workflows/ci.yml # compile C++, syntax-check Python, smoke test ├── Makefile # make -> cpp/bloomdex ├── pyproject.toml ├── CHANGELOG.md · ROADMAP.md · LICENSE ``` ![lattice](docs/assets/lattice.svg) --- ## Preparing the bench (build the microscope) The Python botanist needs nothing but a standard Python 3.8+ interpreter. The C++ microscope must be ground from its single translation unit. Pick either door — both call the compiler directly, no CMake in sight. ```bash # Door 1: Makefile make # produces cpp/bloomdex # Door 2: the build script (auto-detects clang++ or g++) bash cpp/build.sh # Door 3: by hand, if you enjoy the sound of it g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic cpp/bloomdex.cpp -o cpp/bloomdex ``` On Windows with MinGW the same one-liner works; the resulting binary is `cpp/bloomdex.exe`, and the Python bridge already knows to look for the `.exe` suffix. If a build complains about `std::unordered_multimap`, it predates the `` include fix - pull latest and rebuild. --- ## A first pressing (the exact reading) You do not need the microscope to get an exact answer on modest specimens. The botanist can read venation directly: ```bash python -m benchbloom scan \ --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \ --subject examples/training.jsonl \ --field text --ngram 4 --threshold 0.3 ``` This prints a JSON report to stdout and a one-line **verdict** to stderr. In the shipped example, benchmark items `b1`, `b2`, and `b4` were quietly transplanted into the training set, and the scan will flag them with high containment. Items `b3` (a fact about prime numbers) and `b5` (an invented city) never took root and stay clean. The report looks like this: ```json { "summary": { "ref_items": 5, "flagged_pairs": 3, "contaminated_ref_items": 3, "contamination_rate": 0.6, "peak_overlap": 1.0 }, "pairs": [ { "ref_id": "b1", "subject_id": "t5", "jaccard": 0.72, "containment": 1.0 }, ... ] } ``` The **verdict** grades the contamination rate on a simple herbarium scale: - `CLEAN` — nothing germinated above threshold. - `TRACE` — an isolated seedling; inspect the flagged pairs by hand. - `ELEVATED` — meaningful contamination; the benchmark is compromised in part. - `HEAVY` — the specimen is overgrown; treat scores from it with suspicion. --- ## The microscope reading (MinHash at scale) Exact shingling is O(unique-shingles) in memory and quadratic in specimens. When the corpus grows past comfort, hand it to the microscope. The `index` subcommand orchestrates the whole assay: press both specimens, take their spore prints, and overlay the prints. ```bash python -m benchbloom index \ --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \ --subject examples/training.jsonl \ --field text --k 128 --ngram 4 --threshold 0.4 \ --out match.tsv python -m benchbloom report match.tsv ``` Under the hood the botanist: 1. Loads and normalizes both corpora, writing one dried record per line. 2. Calls `bloomdex sign` on each to produce a signature file — `K` 64-bit min-hashes per record, drawn from `K` universal hash seeds over the record's shingle set. 3. Calls `bloomdex match` to compare every reference print against every subject print, emitting a TSV of pairs whose *estimated* Jaccard clears the threshold. The estimate is honest but approximate. The variance of a MinHash Jaccard estimate shrinks roughly with `1/√K`, so `--k 128` gives you a standard error near 0.09 and `--k 512` roughly halves it. When in doubt, confirm a flagged pair with the exact `scan`. The microscope finds candidates; the botanist confirms the diagnosis. ### Reading a spore print by hand You can drive the microscope directly, without the botanist, if you already have normalized text (one record per line): ```bash cpp/bloomdex sign --input ref.norm.txt --out ref.sig --k 256 --ngram 5 cpp/bloomdex sign --input sub.norm.txt --out sub.sig --k 256 --ngram 5 cpp/bloomdex match --ref ref.sig --subject sub.sig --out match.tsv --threshold 0.5 # find near-duplicates *within* a single corpus (deduplication) cpp/bloomdex self --input sub.sig --out dups.tsv --threshold 0.8 ``` A signature line is deliberately plain text so you can inspect it with any tool: ``` r423188823... 199... 40.. (K space-separated 64-bit min-hashes) ``` --- ## How the spore print is actually taken For the curious, here is the honest mechanism, no hand-waving: - **Shingles.** Each normalized record is split into tokens; every window of `ngram` consecutive tokens is joined with a unit-separator byte (`0x1f`) to form one shingle. The separator prevents `["a","bc"]` and `["ab","c"]` from colliding into the same string. - **Base hash.** Each shingle is hashed with 64-bit FNV-1a into a base value. - **Permutations.** `K` universal hash functions of the form `(a·x + b) mod (2⁶¹−1)` permute that base value. The coefficients `a, b` come from a `splitmix64` stream seeded deterministically, so two runs on two machines produce identical prints — a property you want in forensics. - **Min selection.** For each of the `K` functions we keep the minimum permuted value across all shingles. That vector of `K` minima is the signature. - **Estimate.** The estimated Jaccard between two records is simply the fraction of the `K` positions where their minima agree — the classic MinHash identity. Short records (fewer tokens than `ngram`) degrade gracefully: the whole record becomes a single shingle rather than vanishing from the assay. --- ## Command reference ### `benchbloom normalize` Press and dry a corpus into one normalized record per line — the format the microscope consumes. ```bash python -m benchbloom normalize input.jsonl --out dried.txt --field text --field title ``` ### `benchbloom scan` Exact n-gram / Jaccard / containment report, Python only. Flags on containment by default; pass `--jaccard-only` to trigger on Jaccard instead. `--top N` keeps only the N strongest pairs in the JSON body. ### `benchbloom index` Full orchestration through the C++ engine. `--k` sets signature width, `--ngram` the shingle size, `--threshold` the estimated-Jaccard cutoff, `--engine` an explicit path to the binary, and `--workdir` a place to keep intermediates. ### `benchbloom report` Render a saved `match.tsv` into a human summary with the strongest overlaps listed first. ### `bloomdex sign | match | self` The microscope's three lenses: build signatures, compare two signature sets, and find near-duplicates within one set. Run `bloomdex --help` for the exact flags. --- ## Interpreting results without fooling yourself A few honest cautions from the field log: - **Threshold is a dial, not a truth.** A high threshold misses paraphrased leakage; a low one drowns you in coincidental n-gram overlap. Sweep it. - **Containment finds the small-in-large case.** If your benchmark items are short and your training docs are long, prefer the default containment trigger. - **MinHash is a screen, not a verdict.** Treat every flagged pair as a candidate and confirm the important ones with the exact `scan`. - **Normalization changes the answer.** Stripping punctuation merges more items; keeping it (`--keep-punct`) is stricter. Pick one and stay consistent across a study. - **This tool detects textual overlap.** Semantic contamination — the same question rephrased entirely — is out of scope here and always will be for an n-gram instrument. Do not claim more than the spore print shows. --- ## What is honestly finished, and what is not This release is a **foundation**, and the [ROADMAP](ROADMAP.md) says so plainly. Four foundation milestones are implemented and verified: ingestion & normalization, exact leakage metrics, the C++17 MinHash engine, and the Python↔C++ orchestration. Everything past that — LSH banding, binary signature formats, multi-field attribution, HTML reports, threaded signing — is planned, not built. There is no benchmark suite, so no throughput number is claimed as fact; "high-throughput" describes the streaming design, not a measured figure. There are, deliberately, **no unit tests** in this release. The CI instead compiles the C++ engine, syntax-checks every Python module, and runs the example assay end to end as a smoke test. Tests are welcome future work. --- ## License Released under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Press what you like, share the prints freely.
Grown on a quiet bench, one spore print at a time. 🌱

ROADMAP.md.text:
# Roadmap

benchbloom follows a foundation-first plan. The milestones below marked done
are the ones actually implemented and verified in this repository. Everything
under "Planned" is aspirational and not yet built.

## Foundation (verified in this release)

- [x] **M1 — Ingestion & normalization.** JSONL/text loaders with tolerant
  parsing and deterministic NFKC + whitespace/punctuation normalization.
  Implemented in `benchbloom/ingest.py`.
- [x] **M2 — Exact leakage metrics.** Token n-gram shingling with Jaccard and
  containment scoring and a report summarizer. Implemented in
  `benchbloom/metrics.py`.
- [x] **M3 — C++17 MinHash engine.** `bloomdex` builds min-hash signatures over
  token shingles and scores candidate overlap; compiles cleanly with `g++`
  `-std=c++17`. Implemented in `cpp/bloomdex.cpp`.
- [x] **M4 — Python↔C++ orchestration.** The `index` subcommand normalizes,
  signs, and matches through the engine bridge in `benchbloom/engine.py`.

## Planned (not yet implemented)

- [ ] LSH banding to prune the O(N·M) match loop toward near-linear behavior.
- [ ] Streaming signature format with a compact binary encoding.
- [ ] Multi-field weighting and per-field contamination attribution.
- [ ] HTML report export with highlighted overlapping shingles.
- [ ] Parallel signing across shards / threads in the C++ engine.

Honesty note: performance claims for the C++ engine are qualitative
("high-throughput streaming") — no formal benchmark suite ships yet, and none
is claimed here.

SECURITY.md.text:
# Security Policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please do not open a public issue for a security problem. Use GitHub's private
[security advisory](https://github.com/kMegapnbedt/BenchBloom/security/advisories/new) form, or contact a
maintainer directly if the form is unavailable to you.

Include what an attacker gains in one sentence, the version or commit you are running, the smallest
reproduction you can manage, and whether the input is attacker-controlled in your setup. You should
get an acknowledgement within a few working days and a disclosure timeline before anything is
published.

## Scope

benchbloom normalizes untrusted corpora and renders match reports. Malformed JSONL,
oversized records, path handling in `--workdir`/`--out` and TSV report parsing are in
scope; the C++ engine parses files produced by the Python front end.

examples/README.md.text:
# Examples

Two tiny corpora ship here so you can watch benchbloom flag contamination:

- `benchmark.jsonl` — 5 held-out benchmark items (the "reference").
- `training.jsonl` — 6 training documents (the "subject"). Items `t1`, `t2`,
  and `t5` deliberately paraphrase or copy benchmark items `b2`, `b4`, and `b1`.

## Exact Python scan (no compiler needed)

```bash
python -m benchbloom scan \
  --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \
  --subject examples/training.jsonl \
  --field text --ngram 4 --threshold 0.3
```

Pins live in `requirements-dev.txt`; the examples assume the
stock interpreter, no packages required.

You should see `b1`, `b2`, and `b4` flagged with high containment, and a
`verdict:` line printed to stderr.

## MinHash engine path (requires the C++ build)

```bash
# 1) build the engine
make            # or: bash cpp/build.sh

# 2) orchestrate normalize -> sign -> match through bloomdex
python -m benchbloom index \
  --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \
  --subject examples/training.jsonl \
  --field text --k 128 --ngram 4 --threshold 0.4 \
  --out match.tsv

# 3) render the report
python -m benchbloom report match.tsv
```

The estimated Jaccard from MinHash will track (not exactly equal) the exact
scan; raise `--k` to tighten the estimate.

answers.answer: The documents give qualitative verdict descriptions, but no numeric cutoffs or boundary rules: CLEAN means nothing above threshold; TRACE, ELEVATED and HEAVY describe increasing contamination. They do not define the rate formula; the sample shows 5 reference items, 3 contaminated reference items and rate 0.6. They explicitly say scan prints JSON to stdout and a one-line verdict to stderr. Whether other subcommands print verdicts, and where, is not established.

The README command omits --id-field, while its sample report shows ref_id b1 and subject_id t5. The examples guide also says b1, b2 and b4 should be flagged. However, the documents do not explain ID selection, fallback IDs or --id-field. Thus the actual IDs produced by the command, and how to obtain the sample's b1/t5-style IDs, are not established.

The documents do not specify the IDs emitted in match.tsv or report, or whether --id-field survives indexing. They show an illustrative signature beginning with r42, without defining its ID assignment. Index is described as normalizing corpora into one record per line before signing; the general guidance describes --keep-punct. Neither establishes whether punctuation settings carry through all signing stages. Report is only described as a human summary ordered by strongest overlap.

Numeric defaults for n-gram size, thresholds, signature width and --top are not documented. Both README walkthroughs explicitly set scan's ngram=4 and threshold=0.3, and index's k=128, ngram=4 and threshold=0.4, so those commands do not rely on defaults for those parameters. They omit --top; report is invoked with only match.tsv. The scan reference explains what --top N does but gives no default. CONTRIBUTING's scan command omits these numeric options entirely.

The README documents --engine as an explicit binary path, builds producing cpp/bloomdex, and a Python bridge that recognizes the Windows .exe suffix. It does not document the automatic search locations or precedence, missing-binary behavior, or how failures of bloomdex sign/match are handled.

The README only describes --workdir as a place to keep intermediates. It says index writes normalized records and signature files, but does not establish the default directory, intermediate filenames or cleanup behavior. No .gitignore contents or exclusion rules are supplied in the available documents, so excluded build and run outputs cannot be established.

The documents do not explain whether CI was removed or never committed, nor establish a required CI gate. The documents do not state the 5% and 25% cutoffs, calibration evidence, maintainer approval or a policy applying those cutoffs equally to both triggers. README calls the verdict categories a simple scale. It documents scan's default containment trigger and index's estimated-Jaccard threshold separately, and recommends confirming important MinHash candidates with exact scan. That guidance does not establish a shared calibrated verdict standard.

# Contributing

Thanks for looking. A few things that make a change easy to take:

1. Open an issue first for anything larger than a bug fix, so we agree on the shape.
2. Keep the change focused: one behaviour per pull request.
3. Run appropriate checks before opening the PR; the recipe below requires a full source checkout.
4. Add a test for the behaviour you changed. No existing test suite or test runner configuration is supplied in this copy.

README.md.text:
# 🌸 benchbloom **A forensic herbarium for benchmark contamination.** *Press your benchmark between glass, dust it for spores, and read the pollen count where a training corpus brushed against it.* Pipeline: JSONL/text → normalization → exact shingle comparison or C++ MinHash → overlap report.
--- ## Returning to the project Start with the [collaborator handoff](docs/HANDOFF.md) for source-backed behavior, CLI defaults, data formats, limitations, and verification status. This documentation was checked against supplied files only; no build or runtime checks were run. The [example fixtures](examples/README.md#fixture-contents) are preserved in Markdown for readers receiving only documentation. Commands require a full source checkout. ## Field notes before you begin Contamination is quiet. A benchmark item does not announce that it has already been seen during training — it simply germinates, unnoticed, until the day your model scores suspiciously well and you cannot say why. benchbloom is a small, patient instrument for finding those germinated seeds. It treats every corpus like a pressed plant specimen: flatten it, catalogue its parts, and compare the spore prints of two specimens to see whether one grew from the other. There are two instruments on this bench, and they are meant to be used together: - **`benchbloom`** — a pure-Python-standard-library orchestrator. It is the botanist: it collects specimens (JSONL or text), presses and dries them (normalization), and can either read the exact venation of every leaf itself (n-gram / Jaccard) or hand the specimens to the microscope for an approximate reading. - **`bloomdex`** — a C++17 microscope. It grinds each specimen into token shingles, takes a MinHash spore print, and reports where two prints overlap. Signing reads one line at a time; matching holds both signature sets in memory. The Python orchestrator also loads both input corpora into memory. No runtime Python dependencies. No CMake. No test suite shipped (by design — this release is a foundation). Just a botanist, a microscope, and a drawer of honest labels. --- ## Why a botanical metaphor, and why it is not just decoration The metaphor earns its keep because contamination detection genuinely behaves like comparing biological specimens: | Botany | benchbloom | | --- | --- | | Pressing & drying a specimen | Normalization: NFKC, lowercase, retain ASCII letters/digits, collapse whitespace | | A leaf's venation pattern | The set of token n-gram *shingles* of a record | | Two leaves sharing venation | High **Jaccard** / **containment** between shingle sets | | A spore print on paper | A **MinHash signature**: K min-hashes standing in for the whole set | | Matching spore prints under glass | Estimated Jaccard = fraction of matching min-positions | | A short cutting embedded in a larger plant | **Containment**: a benchmark item copied inside a long training doc | Containment is the metaphor that matters most. Real leakage rarely looks like two identical documents. It looks like one small benchmark question pressed flat inside a sprawling web-scraped paragraph. Jaccard punishes that size mismatch; containment does not. benchbloom triggers on containment by default and reports Jaccard alongside it, so you can see both the strict and the sensitive reading. --- ## The bench layout ``` benchbloom/ ├── benchbloom/ # the botanist (pure stdlib Python) │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── __main__.py # python -m benchbloom │ ├── cli.py # normalize | scan | index | report │ ├── ingest.py # JSONL/text loaders + normalization │ ├── metrics.py # exact n-gram shingling, Jaccard, containment │ └── engine.py # bridge to the C++ microscope ├── cpp/ # the microscope (C++17, no deps) │ ├── bloomdex.cpp # sign | match | self │ └── build.sh # direct clang++/g++ build ├── examples/ # two pressed specimens + a walkthrough │ ├── benchmark.jsonl │ ├── training.jsonl │ └── README.md ├── docs/assets/ # two animated SVG plates │ ├── pipeline.svg │ └── lattice.svg ├── docs/HANDOFF.md # collaborator guide and source contracts ├── Makefile # make -> cpp/bloomdex ├── pyproject.toml ├── CHANGELOG.md · ROADMAP.md · LICENSE ``` Exact scanning compares shingle sets; MinHash compares fixed-width signatures. The original SVG illustrations are optional assets and are not needed for this guide. --- ## Preparing the bench (build the microscope) The package declares Python 3.8+ and uses the standard library at runtime; compatibility was not executed in this review. The C++ microscope must be ground from its single translation unit. Pick either door — both call the compiler directly, no CMake in sight. ```bash # Door 1: Makefile make # produces cpp/bloomdex # Door 2: the build script (auto-detects clang++ or g++) bash cpp/build.sh # Door 3: by hand, if you enjoy the sound of it g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic cpp/bloomdex.cpp -o cpp/bloomdex ``` The Python bridge also looks for `cpp/bloomdex.exe`. Windows builds are unverified here; the engine uses the `unsigned __int128` compiler extension. The supplied source includes ``, matching the include fix recorded in the changelog. A current successful build has not been verified. --- ## A first pressing (the exact reading) You do not need the microscope to get an exact answer on modest specimens. The botanist can read venation directly: ```bash python -m benchbloom scan \ --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \ --subject examples/training.jsonl \ --field text --id-field id --ngram 4 --threshold 0.3 ``` The command routes a JSON report to stdout and a one-line **verdict** to stderr. Reading the fixtures and exact metric implementation implies three flagged pairs: `b1/t5`, `b2/t1`, and `b4/t2`, each with containment 1.0. The other reference items have no qualifying overlap at these settings. `--id-field id` retains the fixture IDs; without it, JSON records use generated `jN` IDs. Expected report, derived from the source and fixtures rather than a captured run: ```json { "summary": { "ref_items": 5, "flagged_pairs": 3, "contaminated_ref_items": 3, "contamination_rate": 0.6, "peak_overlap": 1.0 }, "pairs": [ { "ref_id": "b1", "subject_id": "t5", "jaccard": 0.6923, "containment": 1.0 }, { "ref_id": "b2", "subject_id": "t1", "jaccard": 0.5333, "containment": 1.0 }, { "ref_id": "b4", "subject_id": "t2", "jaccard": 0.6923, "containment": 1.0 } ] } ``` The **verdict** grades the contamination rate on a simple herbarium scale: - `CLEAN` — nothing germinated above threshold. - `TRACE` — an isolated seedling; inspect the flagged pairs by hand. - `ELEVATED` — meaningful contamination; the benchmark is compromised in part. - `HEAVY` — the specimen is overgrown; treat scores from it with suspicion. --- ## The microscope reading (MinHash at scale) Exact scanning stores shingle sets and compares every reference/subject pair. MinHash uses fixed-width signatures, but matching still compares every pair and loads both signature files. The `index` subcommand orchestrates normalization, signing, and matching; there is no LSH candidate pruning yet. ```bash python -m benchbloom index \ --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \ --subject examples/training.jsonl \ --field text --k 128 --ngram 4 --threshold 0.4 \ --out match.tsv python -m benchbloom report match.tsv ``` Under the hood the botanist: 1. Loads and normalizes both corpora, writing one dried record per line. 2. Calls `bloomdex sign` on each to produce a signature file — `K` 64-bit min-hashes per record, drawn from `K` universal hash seeds over the record's shingle set. 3. Calls `bloomdex match` to compare every reference print against every subject print, emitting a TSV of pairs whose *estimated* Jaccard clears the threshold. The estimate is approximate. Under ideal independent MinHash sampling, standard error is `sqrt(J*(1-J)/K)`, at most about 0.044 for K=128; K=512 halves that bound. This engine's estimator has not been empirically validated here. Confirm important pairs with exact `scan`; use `--jaccard-only` for the same trigger metric. Containment can find short-in-long overlap that a Jaccard screen misses. Index TSV IDs are generated `rN` line indices, even when `--id-field` is provided. See the [handoff](docs/HANDOFF.md#ingestion-normalization-and-ids) for mapping back to source records and retaining intermediates. ### Reading a spore print by hand You can drive the microscope directly, without the botanist, if you already have normalized text (one record per line): ```bash cpp/bloomdex sign --input ref.norm.txt --out ref.sig --k 256 --ngram 5 cpp/bloomdex sign --input sub.norm.txt --out sub.sig --k 256 --ngram 5 cpp/bloomdex match --ref ref.sig --subject sub.sig --out match.tsv --threshold 0.5 # find near-duplicates *within* a single corpus (deduplication) cpp/bloomdex self --input sub.sig --out dups.tsv --threshold 0.8 ``` A signature line is deliberately plain text so you can inspect it with any tool: ``` r423188823... 199... 40.. (K space-separated 64-bit min-hashes) ``` --- ## How the spore print is actually taken For the curious, here is the honest mechanism, no hand-waving: - **Shingles.** Each normalized record is split into tokens; every window of `ngram` consecutive tokens is joined with a unit-separator byte (`0x1f`) to form one shingle. The separator prevents `["a","bc"]` and `["ab","c"]` from colliding into the same string. - **Base hash.** Each shingle uses an FNV-1a-style 64-bit hash with a nonstandard initial value; see the handoff for signature compatibility details. - **Permutations.** `K` universal hash functions of the form `(a·x + b) mod (2⁶¹−1)` permute that base value. The coefficients `a, b` come from a `splitmix64` stream seeded deterministically, so two runs on two machines are intended to produce identical prints for identical inputs and settings. Cross-platform reproducibility has not been tested in this review. - **Min selection.** For each of the `K` functions we keep the minimum permuted value across all shingles. That vector of `K` minima is the signature. - **Estimate.** The estimated Jaccard between two records is simply the fraction of the `K` positions where their minima agree — the classic MinHash identity. Short records (fewer tokens than `ngram`) degrade gracefully: the whole record becomes a single shingle rather than vanishing from the assay. --- ## Command reference ### `benchbloom normalize` Press and dry a corpus into one normalized record per line — the format the microscope consumes. ```bash python -m benchbloom normalize input.jsonl --out dried.txt --field text --field title ``` ### `benchbloom scan` Exact n-gram / Jaccard / containment report, Python only. Flags on containment by default; pass `--jaccard-only` to trigger on Jaccard instead. `--top N` keeps only the N strongest pairs in the JSON body. ### `benchbloom index` Full orchestration through the C++ engine. `--k` sets signature width, `--ngram` the shingle size, `--threshold` the estimated-Jaccard cutoff, `--engine` an explicit path to the binary, and `--workdir` a place to keep intermediates. ### `benchbloom report` Render a saved `match.tsv` into a human summary with the strongest overlaps listed first. ### `bloomdex sign | match | self` The microscope's three lenses: build signatures, compare two signature sets, and find near-duplicates within one set. Run `bloomdex --help` for the exact flags. --- ## Interpreting results without fooling yourself A few honest cautions from the field log: - **Threshold is a dial, not a truth.** A high threshold misses paraphrased leakage; a low one drowns you in coincidental n-gram overlap. Sweep it. - **Containment finds the small-in-large case.** If your benchmark items are short and your training docs are long, prefer the default containment trigger. - **MinHash is a screen, not a verdict.** Treat every flagged pair as a candidate and confirm the important ones with the exact `scan`. - **Normalization changes the answer.** Default normalization removes non-ASCII letters as well as punctuation. `--keep-punct` exists only on `normalize`; `scan` and `index` always apply default normalization. Record the settings. - **This tool detects textual overlap.** Semantic contamination — the same question rephrased entirely — is out of scope here and always will be for an n-gram instrument. Do not claim more than the spore print shows. --- ## What is honestly finished, and what is not This release is a **foundation**, and the [ROADMAP](ROADMAP.md) says so plainly. Four foundation components are present in the supplied source: ingestion & normalization, exact leakage metrics, the C++17 MinHash engine, and the Python↔C++ orchestration. Everything past that — LSH banding, binary signature formats, multi-field attribution, HTML reports, threaded signing — is planned, not built. There is no benchmark suite, so no throughput number is claimed as fact. Only direct signing is line-streamed; the full pipeline is not. No unit tests or CI workflow are present in the supplied file listing. Earlier documentation describes CI compilation, Python syntax checks, and an example smoke test, but `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is absent from this copy. These checks were not run during documentation review. See [CONTRIBUTING](CONTRIBUTING.md) for a validation recipe to use with a full checkout. --- ## License Released under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Press what you like, share the prints freely.
Grown on a quiet bench, one spore print at a time. 🌱

SECURITY.md.text:
# Security Policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please do not open a public issue for a security problem. Use GitHub's private
[security advisory](https://github.com/kMegapnbedt/BenchBloom/security/advisories/new) form, or contact a
maintainer directly if the form is unavailable to you.

Include what an attacker gains in one sentence, the version or commit you are running, the smallest
reproduction you can manage, and whether the input is attacker-controlled in your setup. You should
get an acknowledgement within a few working days and a disclosure timeline before anything is
published.

## Scope

benchbloom normalizes untrusted corpora and renders match reports. Malformed JSONL,
oversized records, path handling in `--workdir`/`--out` and TSV report parsing are in
scope; the C++ engine parses files produced by the Python front end.

# Returning collaborator handoff

This guide records the supplied benchbloom 0.1.0 source as inspected on 2026-11-14. It is a static review: no commands, builds, tests, installers, or network requests were run. Runtime compatibility, compiler success, performance, and hosted CI status remain unverified.

The documentation-only handoff excludes source, configuration, JSONL fixtures, SVG assets, and dot-paths. This guide preserves their relevant contracts; the fixture contents are embedded in [examples/README.md](../examples/README.md). Commands below require a full source checkout. Source paths are provenance references, not files guaranteed to accompany this handoff.

## Start here

benchbloom detects textual benchmark overlap against a training corpus. It does not establish that a model trained on the text, and it does not detect arbitrary semantic paraphrases. The reference is the benchmark; the subject is the training corpus. Direction matters for containment.

- [README](../README.md): introduction and command walkthrough.
- [Examples](../examples/README.md): recoverable fixtures and expected exact-scan behavior.
- [Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md): existing contribution conventions, tool pin, and proposed checks.
- [Roadmap](../ROADMAP.md): implemented foundation versus planned features.
- [Changelog](../CHANGELOG.md): historical release claims; not evidence of a successful current run.
- [Security](../SECURITY.md), [Support](../SUPPORT.md), and [Code of conduct](../CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md): reporting and community guidance.
- [LICENSE](../LICENSE): MIT, copyright 2026 benchbloom contributors.

## Architecture and ownership

| Source | Responsibility and important entry points |
| --- | --- |
| `benchbloom/__init__.py` | `__version__ = "0.1.0"` |
| `benchbloom/__main__.py` | Module entry point calls `cli.main()` and exits with its result |
| `benchbloom/cli.py` | `build_parser`, command handlers, output routing, verdict categories |
| `benchbloom/ingest.py` | `Record`, `load`, JSONL/text readers, `normalize`, `write_normalized` |
| `benchbloom/metrics.py` | Shingle sets, exact Jaccard/containment, all-pairs matching, summary |
| `benchbloom/engine.py` | Binary discovery, subprocess bridge for `sign`/`match`, TSV parsing |
| `cpp/bloomdex.cpp` | Tokenization, deterministic signatures, `sign`, `match`, `self` |
| `Makefile`, `cpp/build.sh` | Direct compiler builds; no CMake |
| `pyproject.toml` | Packaging metadata, console entry point, declared Python version |

Exact flow: `load` both corpora → normalize text → dictionary of ID to shingle set → compare every nonempty reference/subject pair → summary plus JSON pairs.

Approximate flow: locate engine → load both corpora → write normalized lines → sign each corpus → compare signatures → TSV → verdict. `report` reads an existing TSV; it does not recompute scores.

There is no LSH index despite the command name `index`. Python ingestion materializes both corpora. C++ `sign` processes one line at a time but holds that line's tokens. C++ `match` loads both signature sets and compares all N×M pairs, each using K signature entries; `self` compares every i<j pair. Do not assume the complete pipeline handles corpora larger than memory. There are no supplied throughput measurements.

## Environment and build contract

`pyproject.toml` declares Python >=3.8, version 0.1.0, alpha status, no runtime dependencies, and setuptools >=61.0 as its build dependency. The console script is `benchbloom = benchbloom.cli:main`; `python -m benchbloom` is the source-tree entry point. Only the Python package is listed for setuptools; no configuration bundles or compiles the C++ engine. The package's homepage/changelog URLs use `example.invalid` placeholders.

The supplied Python code uses postponed annotations. The declared minimum version has not been runtime-tested in this review. Runtime uses the Python standard library; packaging and optional lint tooling have separate dependencies.

From a full checkout, the documented build choices are:

```bash
make
# Alternative, chooses clang++ before g++ unless CXX is set:
bash cpp/build.sh
# Equivalent explicit compiler invocation:
g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic cpp/bloomdex.cpp -o cpp/bloomdex
```

The Makefile uses `CXX ?= g++`, overridable `CXXFLAGS`, source `cpp/bloomdex.cpp`, and output `cpp/bloomdex`. `make clean` removes that output and its `.exe` variant. The script uses `CXX` if set, otherwise compiler discovery, and fixed flags matching the command above.

The engine includes `<unordered_map>`, consistent with the unreleased include fix in the changelog. It also uses `unsigned __int128`, a compiler extension; generic C++17 or Windows support is not established by this review. Discovery recognizes `.exe`, but that does not verify a Windows build.

## CLI contract

All defaults below come from `cli.build_parser`. `--version` is a global option.

| Command | Required arguments | Optional arguments and defaults |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `normalize` | positional input, `--out` | repeatable `--field`; `--id-field`; `--keep-punct` false |
| `scan` | `--ref`, `--subject` | `--field`; `--id-field`; `--ngram 5`; `--threshold 0.3`; `--top 0`; `--jaccard-only` false; `--out` |
| `index` | `--ref`, `--subject` | `--field`; `--id-field`; `--ngram 5`; `--k 128`; `--threshold 0.5`; `--engine`; `--workdir`; `--out` |
| `report` | positional TSV input | `--top 10` |

`scan` sends JSON to stdout, or writes it to `--out` and prints a destination message to stdout. Its verdict goes to stderr. `index` prints engine status and the match destination to stdout, and a verdict to stderr; it does not emit the exact scan's JSON summary. `normalize` prints its record count and destination. `report` prints pair count, distinct reference-ID count, and top estimated Jaccards; it cannot calculate a contamination rate because the TSV has no total-reference count.

`scan --top N` limits only the JSON pair list; the summary still describes every flagged pair. Zero means all pairs. Ranking is descending `max(jaccard, containment)`, even with `--jaccard-only`. `report --top N` slices descending Jaccards, so zero means no displayed overlaps. Avoid negative values: the Python handlers use ordinary slicing rather than meaningful negative-top validation.

A successful `scan` or `index` returns 0 even for a HEAVY verdict. `index` returns 3 if no engine is found; there is no automatic exact-scan fallback. Argparse handles usage errors. Other Python file/parse/subprocess failures can propagate as exceptions. C++ explicitly returns 2 for missing required arguments/unknown commands and 3 for handled I/O failures; malformed numeric input can throw uncaught exceptions. Neither interface comprehensively validates parameter ranges. Use positive n-gram size and signature width and thresholds in [0,1].

## Ingestion, normalization, and IDs

Evidence: `ingest.py`, `metrics.build_shingle_index`, `cli._cmd_index`, and `cpp/bloomdex.cpp:cmd_sign`.

- Suffixes `.jsonl`, `.json`, and `.ndjson` (case-insensitive) select line-oriented JSON parsing. A `.json` file is not loaded as a whole JSON array/document. Other suffixes select text, one nonblank line per record. Reads use UTF-8.
- JSON blank lines and malformed JSON lines are silently skipped, with no warning/count. Non-object JSON values are wrapped as a `text` value using Python string conversion.
- Default text field is `text`. Repeated `--field` arguments concatenate fields in the specified order using spaces. String values are included; list/tuple values contribute string, integer, or float elements. Scalar numeric fields and nested objects are ignored. Missing fields yield empty text. Field names are direct keys, not nested paths. Shingles can cross concatenated field boundaries.
- JSON IDs default to `j0`, `j1`, etc. using the zero-based original physical line number, including skipped lines. Use `--id-field id` to retain fixture IDs such as `b1` and `t5`; missing ID keys fall back to `jN`, and values are converted to strings. Plain-text IDs are `tN` from physical line numbers.
- Exact indexing is a dictionary keyed by ID. Duplicate IDs overwrite earlier records; summary `ref_items` counts dictionary entries, including entries with empty shingle sets. Use unique IDs when interpreting rates.
- Normalization does NFKC, lowercasing, replacement of everything outside ASCII `0-9`, `a-z`, and space with spaces, then whitespace collapse and trim. This removes non-ASCII letters as well as punctuation. It is not multilingual Unicode-preserving tokenization.
- Only `normalize` exposes `--keep-punct`. `scan` and `index` always use default normalization. Passing a punctuation-preserving file through either normalizes it again; direct C++ signing also splits on non-alphanumeric bytes.
- `write_normalized` creates parent directories and writes one line per loaded record, including empty normalized records, with no IDs or metadata.
- C++ signing assigns `rN` from the zero-based normalized-file line number and skips tokenless lines, leaving gaps. Thus `index --id-field id` still cannot preserve source IDs in TSV. No ID sidecar is created. Map rows back through loaded-record order, accounting for JSON lines discarded during ingestion. With the supplied fixtures, `r0/r4` corresponds to `b1/t5`, `r1/r0` to `b2/t1`, and `r3/r1` to `b4/t2`.

## Exact metrics and verdicts

Python splits normalized text on whitespace and creates a set of token windows joined by `\x1f`. Repeated shingles count once. A nonempty record shorter than n becomes one whole-record shingle; an empty record produces an empty set. Nonpositive n raises `ValueError`.

For reference set A and subject set B:

- Jaccard = |A∩B| / |A∪B|; both empty gives 0.
- Containment = |A∩B| / |A|; empty A gives 0.
- Matching skips either empty set. Default triggering is containment >= threshold; `--jaccard-only` changes the trigger to Jaccard. Thresholding uses full values before output is rounded to four decimals.

Each JSON pair has `ref_id`, `subject_id`, `jaccard`, and `containment`. Summary keys are `ref_items`, `flagged_pairs`, `contaminated_ref_items`, `contamination_rate`, and `peak_overlap`. Rate is distinct flagged reference IDs divided by reference count, rounded to four decimals (0 for an empty corpus). Exact peak is the maximum of both metrics across flagged pairs; index peak uses estimated Jaccard. Index's denominator is the loaded reference-record count, including records that produce no signature.

Verdicts use the rounded rate: CLEAN at 0, TRACE for 0<rate<0.05, ELEVATED for 0.05<=rate<0.25, HEAVY for rate>=0.25. A CLEAN result can also reflect empty inputs, skipped malformed JSON, or text removed by normalization. These are overlap categories, not proof of model training history.

## Engine discovery, intermediates, and formats

`find_engine` uses this order:

1. Explicit `--engine` path if provided: existence only; a missing explicit path stops discovery.
2. `bloomdex` on PATH.
3. Paths relative to the Python package's parent: `cpp/bloomdex`, `cpp/bloomdex.exe`, `build/bloomdex`, `build/bloomdex.exe`.

Local/explicit checks do not establish executable permission. An absolute explicit path avoids ambiguity for a bare relative filename. `_run` captures output; a nonzero child return raises `EngineError` containing its stderr. The Python bridge provides `sign` and `match`; `self` is available directly in C++ only, despite the bridge module's broader introductory wording.

`index --workdir DIR` creates/reuses DIR and writes `ref.norm.txt`, `subject.norm.txt`, `ref.sig`, and `subject.sig`. Match output defaults to `DIR/match.tsv` or the requested `--out`. Reusing a directory overwrites these fixed names. Without `--workdir`, `tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="benchbloom_")` creates a system temporary directory that the command does not automatically remove. Keep runs separate and retain normalization parameters and source-ID mapping when reproducibility matters. Parents of arbitrary scan/report output paths are not generally created by the writers.

Direct engine options:

| Command | Required | Defaults / optional |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sign` | `--input`, `--out` | `--k 128`, `--ngram 5`, `--min-token 1`, `--seed 0` |
| `match` | `--ref`, `--subject`, `--out` | `--threshold 0.5`, `--top 0` |
| `self` | `--input`, `--out` | `--threshold 0.8` |

`sign` lowercases alphanumeric bytes and filters short tokens with `--min-token`. Seed 0 selects internal seed `0xB100D`. Python index uses min-token 1 and seed 0, with no CLI switches for either. The signing diagnostic counts input lines, including skipped tokenless records, rather than actual signatures.

Signature files have no header and contain `id<TAB>token_count<TAB>h0 h1 ... hK-1`, with decimal unsigned 64-bit hash values. They contain no schema version, seed, n-gram size, or normalization metadata. Keep those settings externally and identical across corpora. Width mismatches return similarity 0; seed or n-gram mismatches are not detected. Token count is recorded but not used to estimate containment.

`match` writes header `ref_id<TAB>subject_id<TAB>jaccard` and every pair at or above threshold, in input traversal order. Its `--top` flag is parsed but has no effect: the branch does not emit or limit rows. `self` writes `id_a<TAB>id_b<TAB>jaccard`, compares i<j, and excludes self-pairs. The Python TSV parser discards the first line without validating its header, ignores rows not having exactly three tab-separated fields, and parses the third field with `float`. Headerless input loses its first row; invalid numeric values raise. It can parse the three-column self report, but `report` then labels the first column as reference IDs.

## Hash compatibility and approximation limits

The engine uses a multiply/XOR hash labeled FNV-1a, with initial value `1469598103934665603` and multiplier `1099511628211`. That initial value differs from the standard 64-bit FNV-1a offset basis; preserve it when reproducing existing signatures. SplitMix64 produces coefficient pairs; each permutation computes `(a*(x mod p)+b) mod p`, p=2^61−1, using a 128-bit intermediate. Each position keeps its minimum and the score is the fraction of equal positions.

C++ normal windows append a unit-separator after every token, including the last. Its short-record path appends spaces, including a trailing space. Python joins with unit-separators without a trailing separator. Do not assume byte-identical shingles across implementations or standard third-party signature interoperability. In particular, the short-record encoding can differ from the same token sequence used as a full window under a different n-gram setting.

Under the ideal independent MinHash model, standard error is sqrt(J(1−J)/K), at most about 0.044 at K=128; variance scales as 1/K. This implementation's hash family has not been statistically validated here. Increasing K reduces expected sampling noise, not the difference between containment and Jaccard. Long subject documents may have high containment and low Jaccard, so MinHash screening can miss pairs found by default exact scanning. Compare with `scan --jaccard-only` using matching normalization and n-gram settings when evaluating Jaccard estimates.

## Verification state and unresolved work

The source listing contains no tests, benchmark suite, or `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, although the original README and historical changelog describe CI. Current hosted CI and past successful build claims cannot be established from this copy. The listed `.github/dependabot.yml` configures weekly pip updates at `/` with an open-PR limit of 3; `requirements-dev.txt` pins `ruff==0.7.0`. No Ruff invocation or project-specific Ruff settings were supplied.

Source supports the four foundation components listed in the roadmap. LSH banding, binary signatures, field weighting/attribution, HTML reports, and parallel signing are planned, not implemented. Concrete current limitations include source-ID loss in index output, lossy non-ASCII normalization, duplicate-ID overwrites in scan, unvalidated signature metadata, and ineffective C++ `match --top`. This documentation does not change their implementation.

The check commands and targeted cases in [CONTRIBUTING](../CONTRIBUTING.md) are a future validation recipe for a full checkout, not successful results from this review. No unreadable oversized source lines were encountered. Remaining uncertainty is runtime behavior and external project state, not a silently inferred file read.
