# Examples

Two tiny corpora were supplied with this project:

- `benchmark.jsonl`: 5 reference benchmark items.
- `training.jsonl`: 6 subject training documents. Items `t1`, `t2`, and `t5` contain the text of benchmark items `b2`, `b4`, and `b1`, respectively.

The commands below are a recipe for a full source checkout, not a record of executed checks. This documentation review ran no project code. Readers receiving only Markdown can recover the fixtures from the final section, but also need the source to run the commands. Run from the project root.

## Exact Python scan (no compiler needed)

```bash
python -m benchbloom scan \
  --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \
  --subject examples/training.jsonl \
  --field text --id-field id --ngram 4 --threshold 0.3
```

The Python runtime uses only the standard library. Optional lint tooling is pinned to `ruff==0.7.0` in `requirements-dev.txt`; it is not required to run the example.

`--id-field id` is necessary to retain `bN`/`tN` IDs. Without it, both JSONL files use generated `jN` IDs based on zero-based physical line numbers.

Expected results below are derived by reading the fixtures and exact shingle implementation, not captured runtime output. Each copied reference has all of its four-token shingles present in its subject; the listed sets contain no repeated shingles.

| Reference / subject | Shared / union shingles | Jaccard | Containment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `b1` / `t5` | 9 / 13 | 0.6923 | 1.0 |
| `b2` / `t1` | 8 / 15 | 0.5333 | 1.0 |
| `b4` / `t2` | 9 / 13 | 0.6923 | 1.0 |

At these settings the expected summary is 5 reference items, 3 flagged pairs, 3 contaminated reference items, rate 0.6, and peak overlap 1.0. No other pair shares a four-token shingle. The verdict category is HEAVY, printed to stderr; the JSON goes to stdout unless `--out` is supplied. The command's success exit code does not indicate a clean benchmark.

Defaults differ from this example: `scan` uses `--ngram 5` and `--threshold 0.3`. `--top` limits displayed pairs without changing the summary. See the [handoff](../docs/HANDOFF.md) for all defaults and edge cases.

## MinHash engine path (requires the C++ build)

```bash
make
# Alternative build: bash cpp/build.sh

python -m benchbloom index \
  --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \
  --subject examples/training.jsonl \
  --field text --k 128 --ngram 4 --threshold 0.4 \
  --out match.tsv

python -m benchbloom report match.tsv
```

Index estimates Jaccard; the default exact scan triggers on containment. Their flagged pairs need not agree. Raise K to reduce expected sampling noise, and use exact `scan --jaccard-only` with the same n-gram size to compare Jaccard scores. No estimated scores or engine build results were verified in this review.

The TSV has `ref_id`, `subject_id`, and `jaccard` columns. Index loses original JSON IDs during normalized-file output, so even `--id-field id` cannot preserve them here. Fixture mappings are:

| Source pair | Engine pair |
| --- | --- |
| `b1` / `t5` | `r0` / `r4` |
| `b2` / `t1` | `r1` / `r0` |
| `b4` / `t2` | `r3` / `r1` |

Use a separate `--workdir` for each run to retain `ref.norm.txt`, `subject.norm.txt`, `ref.sig`, and `subject.sig`. Without it, index creates a temporary directory and does not clean it up. It reports the TSV destination but does not output the exact scan's JSON summary. `report` shows counts and strongest pairs; it has no denominator for a contamination rate.

## Fixture contents

These are verbatim contents of the supplied fixture files, retained because JSONL files are excluded from the documentation-only handoff. The fixture wording is test data, not a scientific claim.

### examples/benchmark.jsonl

```jsonl
{"id": "b1", "text": "The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the plant cell and drives respiration."}
{"id": "b2", "text": "Photosynthesis converts sunlight water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen."}
{"id": "b3", "text": "A prime number greater than two is always odd because two divides all even numbers."}
{"id": "b4", "text": "Xylem transports water upward while phloem distributes sugars throughout the vascular plant."}
{"id": "b5", "text": "The capital of the fictional republic of Verdania is the coastal city of Aloravel."}
```

### examples/training.jsonl

```jsonl
{"id": "t1", "text": "Today we learned that photosynthesis converts sunlight water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen for the leaf."}
{"id": "t2", "text": "Gardeners know that xylem transports water upward while phloem distributes sugars throughout the vascular plant tissue."}
{"id": "t3", "text": "The chef prepared a wonderful risotto with saffron and aged parmesan on a rainy autumn evening."}
{"id": "t4", "text": "Rockets rely on Newton's third law: every action produces an equal and opposite reaction in the exhaust plume."}
{"id": "t5", "text": "The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the plant cell and drives respiration inside every living tissue."}
{"id": "t6", "text": "A weekly farmers market sells heirloom tomatoes basil and fresh cut sunflowers near the old stone bridge."}
```

answers.answer: Verdicts use the contamination rate rounded to four decimals: CLEAN = 0; TRACE = 0 < rate < 0.05; ELEVATED = 0.05 ≤ rate < 0.25; HEAVY = rate ≥ 0.25. Rate is distinct flagged reference IDs divided by reference count, or 0 for an empty corpus. Scan counts reference entries after ID-based dictionary indexing, including empty shingle sets; duplicate IDs overwrite earlier records. Index uses the loaded reference-record count, including records producing no signature. Scan and index print verdicts to stderr. Normalize and report do not print verdicts; report lacks the total-reference denominator needed to calculate a rate.

The saved README's command already includes --id-field id. As written, its expected report uses b1/t5, b2/t1 and b4/t2. These are documented expectations derived from fixtures and implementation, not captured execution. Without --id-field id, JSONL IDs use zero-based physical line numbers: the corresponding pairs would be j0/j4, j1/j0 and j3/j1. Add --id-field id to a command lacking it to retain the bN/tN fixture IDs.

Index signatures and match.tsv use rN IDs from zero-based normalized-file line numbers. Report reads those TSV IDs without restoring source IDs. Tokenless lines are skipped during signing, leaving gaps; map IDs through loaded-record order, accounting for discarded JSON lines. Fixture mappings include b1/t5 → r0/r4, b2/t1 → r1/r0 and b4/t2 → r3/r1; these mappings do not establish which pairs pass a particular MinHash threshold. --id-field does not survive normalized-file writing, which stores no IDs or metadata; no ID sidecar is created. Index always applies default normalization, removing punctuation and non-ASCII letters. --keep-punct exists only on normalize; index normalizes its input again, and direct C++ signing also splits on non-alphanumeric bytes.

Defaults: scan uses ngram=5, threshold=0.3 (containment), top=0 (all pairs), and no signature-width option. Index uses ngram=5, threshold=0.5 (estimated Jaccard), k=128, and exposes no --top option. Report uses top=10 and has no ngram, threshold or signature-width setting. Scan's --top limits displayed pairs without changing summary counts; report --top 0 displays no overlaps. The README/example scan commands explicitly set ngram=4 and threshold=0.3, relying on the default top=0. Their index commands explicitly set ngram=4, threshold=0.4 and k=128; only k matches its default. Their report commands rely on top=10. Separately, direct bloomdex match defaults to --top 0, but that flag has no effect.

Discovery checks: (1) an explicit --engine path, checking existence only; a missing explicit path stops discovery; (2) bloomdex on PATH; (3) cpp/bloomdex, cpp/bloomdex.exe, build/bloomdex and build/bloomdex.exe relative to the Python package's parent, in that order. Local/explicit existence checks do not verify executable permission. If no engine is found, index returns 3, without an automatic exact-scan fallback. The subprocess bridge captures output; a nonzero bloomdex return raises EngineError containing its stderr. Python subprocess/file/parse failures can propagate as exceptions.

The intermediate-file behavior is established: without --workdir, index uses tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="benchbloom_") to create a system temporary directory and does not automatically remove it. It writes ref.norm.txt, subject.norm.txt, ref.sig and subject.sig there; match.tsv also defaults there unless --out specifies another destination. The saved documents do not establish which outputs .gitignore excludes. The handoff explicitly excludes configuration and dot-paths, and does not preserve .gitignore's patterns; generated outputs cannot be assumed to be ignored.

The documents do not establish whether CI was intentionally removed, never committed, or is expected to gate changes. The changelog records a CI workflow as added, while the handoff and contribution guide say .github/workflows/ci.yml is absent and current CI behavior is unknown. CONTRIBUTING requires appropriate checks before opening a PR, but that does not establish an automated CI gate.

The documents establish implemented verdict boundaries, not calibration, maintainer approval, or an intended scientific standard applying equally to both triggers. They document the same rate categories for scan/index, while scan defaults to containment and index screens estimated Jaccard; their flagged pairs can differ. The handoff calls verdicts overlap categories rather than proof of training history and says the MinHash hash family has not been statistically validated here. Shared implementation therefore does not establish equal validity or approved interpretation across the two paths.

All notable changes to benchbloom are documented here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and the project aims

  contributing guide.

  compile on a clean checkout because `std::unordered_multimap` was used
  without its header.

## [0.1.0] - 2026-09-01

### Added
- Pure-stdlib Python orchestrator (`benchbloom`) with `normalize`, `scan`,
  `index`, and `report` subcommands.
- JSONL / text ingestion with tolerant parsing and NFKC-based normalization.
- Exact n-gram shingling with Jaccard and containment leakage metrics.
- C++17 engine `bloomdex` implementing token-shingle MinHash signatures and
  candidate overlap scoring (`sign`, `match`, `self`).
- Direct `g++`/`clang++` build via `Makefile` and `cpp/build.sh` (no CMake).
- Worked examples: reference/subject corpora and an end-to-end walkthrough.
- CI workflow compiling the C++ engine and syntax-checking the Python package.

### Notes
- MinHash overlap is an estimate; use `scan` for exact verification on small
  corpora. Estimator variance narrows as `--k` increases.

# 🌸 benchbloom **A forensic herbarium for benchmark contamination.** *Press your benchmark between glass, dust it for spores, and read the pollen count where a training corpus brushed against it.* The workflow is: **ingest → normalize → exact scan**, or **normalize → MinHash sign → match → report**.
--- Returning collaborators: start with [project context](docs/context.md) for the source-backed state, contracts, verification gaps and documentation map. ## Field notes before you begin Contamination is quiet. A benchmark item does not announce that it has already been seen during training — it simply germinates, unnoticed, until the day your model scores suspiciously well and you cannot say why. benchbloom is a small, patient instrument for finding those germinated seeds. It treats every corpus like a pressed plant specimen: flatten it, catalogue its parts, and compare the spore prints of two specimens to see whether one grew from the other. There are two instruments on this bench, and they are meant to be used together: - **`benchbloom`** — a pure-Python-standard-library orchestrator. It is the botanist: it collects specimens (JSONL or text), presses and dries them (normalization), and can either read the exact venation of every leaf itself (n-gram / Jaccard) or hand the specimens to the microscope for a faster, approximate reading. - **`bloomdex`** — a C++17 microscope. It grinds each specimen into token shingles, takes a MinHash spore print, and reports where two prints overlap. Signing processes one line at a time. Matching loads both signature sets into memory, and the Python orchestrator loads both corpora; the full pipeline is not a bounded-memory stream. No external libraries. No CMake. No test suite shipped (by design — this release is a foundation). Just a botanist, a microscope, and a drawer of honest labels. --- ## Why a botanical metaphor, and why it is not just decoration The metaphor earns its keep because contamination detection genuinely behaves like comparing biological specimens: | Botany | benchbloom | | --- | --- | | Pressing & drying a specimen | Normalization: NFKC fold, lowercase, collapse whitespace, drop punctuation | | A leaf's venation pattern | The set of token n-gram *shingles* of a record | | Two leaves sharing venation | High **Jaccard** / **containment** between shingle sets | | A spore print on paper | A **MinHash signature**: K min-hashes standing in for the whole set | | Matching spore prints under glass | Estimated Jaccard = fraction of matching min-positions | | A short cutting embedded in a larger plant | **Containment**: a benchmark item copied inside a long training doc | Containment is the metaphor that matters most. Real leakage rarely looks like two identical documents. It looks like one small benchmark question pressed flat inside a sprawling web-scraped paragraph. Jaccard punishes that size mismatch; containment does not. benchbloom triggers on containment by default and reports Jaccard alongside it, so you can see both the strict and the sensitive reading. --- ## The bench layout ``` benchbloom/ ├── benchbloom/ # the botanist (pure stdlib Python) │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── __main__.py # python -m benchbloom │ ├── cli.py # normalize | scan | index | report │ ├── ingest.py # JSONL/text loaders + normalization │ ├── metrics.py # exact n-gram shingling, Jaccard, containment │ └── engine.py # bridge to the C++ microscope ├── cpp/ # the microscope (C++17, no deps) │ ├── bloomdex.cpp # sign | match | self │ └── build.sh # direct clang++/g++ build ├── examples/ # two pressed specimens + a walkthrough │ ├── benchmark.jsonl │ ├── training.jsonl │ └── README.md ├── docs/assets/ # two animated SVG plates │ ├── pipeline.svg │ └── lattice.svg ├── docs/context.md # returning-collaborator handoff and evidence limits ├── Makefile # make -> cpp/bloomdex ├── pyproject.toml ├── CHANGELOG.md · ROADMAP.md · LICENSE ``` The MinHash comparison counts matching signature positions and divides by the signature width K. The original SVG illustrations are available only in a full checkout containing `docs/assets/`. --- ## Preparing the bench (build the microscope) The Python botanist needs nothing but a standard Python 3.8+ interpreter. The C++ microscope must be ground from its single translation unit. Pick either door — both call the compiler directly, no CMake in sight. ```bash # Door 1: Makefile make # produces cpp/bloomdex # Door 2: the build script (auto-detects clang++ or g++) bash cpp/build.sh # Door 3: by hand, if you enjoy the sound of it g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic cpp/bloomdex.cpp -o cpp/bloomdex ``` The Python bridge also searches for `cpp/bloomdex.exe`. Windows/MinGW build success has not been checked in this copy; the engine uses the compiler extension `unsigned __int128`, so confirm compiler support and select the output filename explicitly when building on that platform. If a build complains about `std::unordered_multimap`, it predates the `` include fix - pull latest and rebuild. --- ## A first pressing (the exact reading) You do not need the microscope to get an exact answer on modest specimens. The botanist can read venation directly: ```bash python -m benchbloom scan \ --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \ --subject examples/training.jsonl \ --field text --id-field id --ngram 4 --threshold 0.3 ``` This command is intended to print a JSON report to stdout and a one-line **verdict** to stderr. The fixture deliberately embeds `b1`, `b2`, and `b4` in the training set; `b3` (prime numbers) and `b5` (an invented city) are the negative examples. `--id-field id` preserves those fixture labels; without it, JSONL IDs default to zero-based `j0`, `j1`, etc. The following is an illustrative report excerpt, not captured execution output. See the [retained fixture and expected relationships](examples/README.md) for source-derived expectations; this documentation review did not run the assay: ```json { "summary": { "ref_items": 5, "flagged_pairs": 3, "contaminated_ref_items": 3, "contamination_rate": 0.6, "peak_overlap": 1.0 }, "pairs": [ { "ref_id": "b1", "subject_id": "t5", "jaccard": 0.6923, "containment": 1.0 }, ... ] } ``` The **verdict** grades the contamination rate on a simple herbarium scale: - `CLEAN` — nothing germinated above threshold. - `TRACE` — an isolated seedling; inspect the flagged pairs by hand. - `ELEVATED` — meaningful contamination; the benchmark is compromised in part. - `HEAVY` — the specimen is overgrown; treat scores from it with suspicion. --- ## The microscope reading (MinHash at scale) Exact scanning stores shingle sets for both corpora and compares every reference against every subject. When the corpus grows past comfort, hand it to the microscope. The `index` subcommand orchestrates the whole assay: press both specimens, take their spore prints, and overlay the prints. ```bash python -m benchbloom index \ --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \ --subject examples/training.jsonl \ --field text --k 128 --ngram 4 --threshold 0.4 \ --out match.tsv python -m benchbloom report match.tsv ``` Under the hood the botanist: 1. Loads and normalizes both corpora, writing one dried record per line. 2. Calls `bloomdex sign` on each to produce a signature file — `K` 64-bit min-hashes per record, drawn from `K` universal hash seeds over the record's shingle set. 3. Calls `bloomdex match` to compare every reference print against every subject print, emitting a TSV of pairs whose *estimated* Jaccard clears the threshold. The estimate is approximate. Under ideal independent MinHash samples, variance is J(1−J)/K and standard error scales with `1/√K`; increasing K from 128 to 512 halves that standard error. This is estimator theory, not an empirical error bound measured for this engine. Confirm important candidates with exact `scan`, and use `--jaccard-only` when comparing the same metric. `index` uses generated `r0`, `r1`, etc. IDs; retain input order to map results back to original records. ### Reading a spore print by hand You can drive the microscope directly, without the botanist, if you already have normalized text (one record per line): ```bash cpp/bloomdex sign --input ref.norm.txt --out ref.sig --k 256 --ngram 5 cpp/bloomdex sign --input sub.norm.txt --out sub.sig --k 256 --ngram 5 cpp/bloomdex match --ref ref.sig --subject sub.sig --out match.tsv --threshold 0.5 # find near-duplicates *within* a single corpus (deduplication) cpp/bloomdex self --input sub.sig --out dups.tsv --threshold 0.8 ``` A signature line is deliberately plain text so you can inspect it with any tool: ``` r423188823... 199... 40.. (K space-separated 64-bit min-hashes) ``` --- ## How the spore print is actually taken For the curious, here is the honest mechanism, no hand-waving: - **Shingles.** Each normalized record is split into tokens; every window of `ngram` consecutive tokens is joined with a unit-separator byte (`0x1f`) to form one shingle. The separator prevents `["a","bc"]` and `["ab","c"]` from colliding into the same string. - **Base hash.** Each shingle is hashed with an FNV-1a-style 64-bit loop into a base value. The implementation uses a nonstandard offset basis; see the [compatibility finding](docs/context.md#verification-gaps-and-next-work). - **Permutations.** `K` universal hash functions of the form `(a·x + b) mod (2⁶¹−1)` permute that base value. The coefficients `a, b` come from a `splitmix64` stream seeded deterministically, so two runs on two machines are intended to produce identical prints with matching settings and engine implementation. Cross-platform reproducibility was not tested here. - **Min selection.** For each of the `K` functions we keep the minimum permuted value across all shingles. That vector of `K` minima is the signature. - **Estimate.** The estimated Jaccard between two records is simply the fraction of the `K` positions where their minima agree — the classic MinHash identity. Short records (fewer tokens than `ngram`) degrade gracefully: the whole record becomes a single shingle rather than vanishing from the assay. --- ## Command reference ### `benchbloom normalize` Press and dry a corpus into one normalized record per line — the format the microscope consumes. ```bash python -m benchbloom normalize input.jsonl --out dried.txt --field text --field title ``` ### `benchbloom scan` Exact n-gram / Jaccard / containment report, Python only. Flags on containment by default; pass `--jaccard-only` to trigger on Jaccard instead. `--top N` keeps only the N strongest pairs in the JSON body. ### `benchbloom index` Full orchestration through the C++ engine. `--k` sets signature width, `--ngram` the shingle size, `--threshold` the estimated-Jaccard cutoff, `--engine` an explicit path to the binary, and `--workdir` a place to keep intermediates. ### `benchbloom report` Render a saved `match.tsv` into a human summary with the strongest overlaps listed first. ### `bloomdex sign | match | self` The microscope's three lenses: build signatures, compare two signature sets, and find near-duplicates within one set. Run `bloomdex --help` for the exact flags. --- ## Interpreting results without fooling yourself A few honest cautions from the field log: - **Threshold is a dial, not a truth.** A high threshold misses paraphrased leakage; a low one drowns you in coincidental n-gram overlap. Sweep it. - **Containment finds the small-in-large case.** If your benchmark items are short and your training docs are long, prefer the default containment trigger. - **MinHash is a screen, not a verdict.** Treat every flagged pair as a candidate and confirm the important ones with the exact `scan`. - **Normalization changes the answer.** Default normalization removes non-ASCII letters as well as punctuation. Only `normalize` exposes `--keep-punct`; `scan` and `index` always use the default filter, and C++ tokenization splits punctuation again. See the [input contract](docs/context.md#input-and-normalization-contract). - **This tool detects textual overlap.** Semantic contamination — the same question rephrased entirely — is out of scope here and always will be for an n-gram instrument. Do not claim more than the spore print shows. --- ## What is honestly finished, and what is not This release is a **foundation**, and the [ROADMAP](ROADMAP.md) says so plainly. Four foundation milestones have implementations in this copy: ingestion & normalization, exact leakage metrics, the C++17 MinHash engine, and the Python↔C++ orchestration. Everything past that — LSH banding, binary signature formats, multi-field attribution, HTML reports, threaded signing — is planned, not built. There is no benchmark suite, so no throughput number is claimed as fact; "high-throughput" describes the streaming design, not a measured figure. There are, deliberately, **no unit tests** in this release. Earlier documentation describes CI compiling the engine, syntax-checking Python and running the example assay, but the referenced `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is absent from this supplied copy. No CI or runtime result was verified during this review. Tests are welcome future work; see [contributor checks](CONTRIBUTING.md). --- ## License Released under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Press what you like, share the prints freely.
Grown on a quiet bench, one spore print at a time. 🌱

ROADMAP.md.text:
# Roadmap

benchbloom follows a foundation-first plan. The milestones below marked done
retain the original release's implementation/verification claims. A source-only
review on 2026-11-14 found the corresponding implementations, but did not run
builds or tests; no retained runtime results or CI workflow were available in
this copy. See [current evidence and verification gaps](docs/context.md).
Everything under "Planned" remains aspirational and not yet built.

## Foundation (verified in this release)

- [x] **M1 — Ingestion & normalization.** JSONL/text loaders with tolerant
  parsing and deterministic NFKC + whitespace/punctuation normalization.
  Implemented in `benchbloom/ingest.py`.
- [x] **M2 — Exact leakage metrics.** Token n-gram shingling with Jaccard and
  containment scoring and a report summarizer. Implemented in
  `benchbloom/metrics.py`.
- [x] **M3 — C++17 MinHash engine.** `bloomdex` builds min-hash signatures over
  token shingles and scores candidate overlap; compiles cleanly with `g++`
  `-std=c++17`. Implemented in `cpp/bloomdex.cpp`.
- [x] **M4 — Python↔C++ orchestration.** The `index` subcommand normalizes,
  signs, and matches through the engine bridge in `benchbloom/engine.py`.

## Planned (not yet implemented)

- [ ] LSH banding to prune the O(N·M) match loop toward near-linear behavior.
- [ ] Streaming signature format with a compact binary encoding.
- [ ] Multi-field weighting and per-field contamination attribution.
- [ ] HTML report export with highlighted overlapping shingles.
- [ ] Parallel signing across shards / threads in the C++ engine.

Honesty note: performance claims for the C++ engine are qualitative
("high-throughput streaming") — no formal benchmark suite ships yet, and none
is claimed here.

SECURITY.md.text:
# Security Policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please do not open a public issue for a security problem. Use GitHub's private
[security advisory](https://github.com/kMegapnbedt/BenchBloom/security/advisories/new) form, or contact a
maintainer directly if the form is unavailable to you.

Include what an attacker gains in one sentence, the version or commit you are running, the smallest
reproduction you can manage, and whether the input is attacker-controlled in your setup. You should
get an acknowledgement within a few working days and a disclosure timeline before anything is
published.

## Scope

benchbloom normalizes untrusted corpora and renders match reports. Malformed JSONL,
oversized records, path handling in `--workdir`/`--out` and TSV report parsing are in
scope; the C++ engine parses files produced by the Python front end.

# benchbloom project context

Source review: 2026-11-14. This is a handoff for a returning collaborator.
The supplied Python, C++, configuration and example files were read, but no
commands, builds, tests or network checks were run. Implementation statements
below describe source, not demonstrated runtime results.

## Start here

benchbloom detects textual overlap between a reference benchmark and a subject
training corpus. It offers exact Python n-gram comparisons and an approximate
C++ MinHash path. Semantic paraphrase detection is outside its stated scope.
Overlap is evidence to inspect, not proof that a model trained on a particular item.

- [README](../README.md): purpose, build instructions and CLI walkthrough.
- [Examples](../examples/README.md): commands and complete retained sample inputs.
- [Roadmap](../ROADMAP.md): the existing progress view; four foundation milestones
  are recorded as done, with later features explicitly planned. Preserve that
  checklist rather than starting another tracker.
- [Changelog](../CHANGELOG.md): historical release and unreleased changes.
- [Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md), [security policy](../SECURITY.md),
  [support](../SUPPORT.md) and [code of conduct](../CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md): contribution
  and reporting procedures. License: [MIT](../LICENSE).
- [Agent guidance](../AGENTS.md): context maintenance and setup status.

This document owns the source-backed architecture, contracts and unresolved
verification questions. The roadmap owns feature status; the examples own the
small reproducible fixture. Source paths below are evidence identifiers in the
full checkout. A Markdown-only handoff excludes source, configuration, binaries,
SVG assets and installed skills; it cannot run the documented commands on its
own. The essential fixture and configuration facts are retained here and in the
examples so the reader need not infer them from missing files.

## State and design boundaries

Package metadata and `benchbloom/__init__.py` both declare version `0.1.0`.
The changelog dates that release 2026-09-01 and separately records unreleased
tooling and header fixes; this does not establish publication or deployment.
Metadata declares Python >=3.8, Alpha status and no runtime dependencies.
Build tooling uses setuptools >=61.0; the optional dev pin is `ruff==0.7.0`.
Python-version compatibility has not been exercised in this review.

The documented foundation-first approach uses Python's standard library and one
C++ translation unit with direct compiler builds, avoiding external runtime
libraries and CMake. The default exact trigger is containment because a small
benchmark item embedded in a longer document can have low Jaccard overlap.
These choices are documented in the README and implemented in source; no separate
owner approval record was supplied.

| Component / evidence | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `benchbloom/__main__.py`, `cli.py:main/build_parser` | Both module execution and the metadata console entry point reach the CLI. Commands are `normalize`, `scan`, `index`, `report`. |
| `ingest.py` | Read records, select fields and IDs, normalize, and emit line-oriented text. |
| `metrics.py` | Build exact shingle sets by ID, compare every pair, summarize contamination. |
| `engine.py` | Find the executable, invoke `sign` and `match`, raise on nonzero exit, parse TSV. There is no Python wrapper for `self` in this copy. |
| `cpp/bloomdex.cpp` | Tokenize and sign lines; load signatures for all-pairs matching or within-corpus deduplication. |

The C++ signing loop handles one line at a time, but Python `load()` materializes
each corpus and C++ `load_sigs()` materializes signature sets. `match` compares
N × M pairs, with K signature positions per comparison; `self` compares each
unordered pair. The complete pipeline is not bounded-memory streaming, and no
measured throughput or benchmark suite is supplied.

## Input and normalization contract

Evidence: `ingest.py:load/read_jsonl/read_text/normalize/write_normalized`.

- Suffixes `.jsonl`, `.json` and `.ndjson` select line-by-line JSON parsing.
  A `.json` suffix does not select a whole-array JSON loader. Other suffixes
  select plain text with one nonblank line per record.
- JSON blank lines and malformed JSON lines are skipped. Non-object JSON values
  are converted to text records. The default field is `text`; repeated
  `--field` values concatenate fields in argument order. String values are
  retained; list/tuple values contribute string and numeric elements.
  Scalar numeric field values are not added by the field extractor.
- JSON IDs default to `j0`, `j1`, etc., using original zero-based line
  numbers. `--id-field id` selects the fixture's `b1`/`t1` IDs, with a
  line-based fallback if the field is missing. Plain text uses `t0`, `t1`,
  etc. Skipped input lines can leave gaps in default IDs.
- Normalization applies NFKC, lowercasing, replacement of everything outside
  ASCII `0-9a-z ` with spaces, then whitespace collapse/trim. The default
  thus removes non-ASCII letters as well as punctuation; multilingual content
  can lose meaningful text or become empty.
- Only `normalize` exposes `--keep-punct`; it skips that ASCII filter but
  still applies NFKC, lowercase and whitespace collapse. `scan` and `index`
  always use default normalization. C++ tokenization splits non-alphanumeric
  bytes again, so punctuation-preserving output does not make C++ punctuation-sensitive.
- Normalized output contains text only, including blank lines for records that
  normalize empty. It drops source IDs and metadata. Keep original inputs and
  loading order if mapping C++ results back to records matters.

## Exact scan contract

Evidence: `metrics.py` and `cli.py:_cmd_scan/_print_verdict/build_parser`.

Records become sets of token n-grams joined with a unit separator. A nonempty
record shorter than n becomes one whole-record shingle; empty records have an
empty set. n <= 0 raises `ValueError`. Repeated IDs overwrite earlier records
in the shingle-index dictionary, so IDs must be unique for a faithful item count.

For reference set A and subject set B:

- Jaccard = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|.
- Containment = |A ∩ B| / |A|, measuring how much of the reference occurs
  in the subject. Empty sets score zero; cross-comparison skips empty sets.
- Defaults: n=5, threshold=0.3, containment trigger. `--jaccard-only`
  switches the trigger, and equality with the threshold counts as a hit.
- Stored scores are rounded to four decimals after threshold comparison.
  Pairs sort descending by max(Jaccard, containment), even in Jaccard-only mode.
- `--top N` truncates only the JSON pairs body. Default 0 retains all pairs.
  The summary always covers all flagged pairs.
- JSON summary keys: `ref_items`, `flagged_pairs`,
  `contaminated_ref_items`, `contamination_rate`, `peak_overlap`.
  `ref_items` counts unique reference IDs, including empty shingle sets.
  Rate is the number of flagged reference IDs divided by that count.
- Without `--out`, JSON goes to stdout. With it, JSON goes to the named file
  and stdout reports its path. The verdict always goes to stderr.

Verdicts use the rounded summary rate: 0 is CLEAN, positive rates below 0.05 are
TRACE, rates from 0.05 to below 0.25 are ELEVATED, and rates >=0.25 are HEAVY.
They classify overlap under the selected settings, not independently established
model contamination.

## MinHash workflow and artifacts

Evidence: `cli.py:_cmd_index`, `engine.py`, and `cpp/bloomdex.cpp`.

1. Resolve the engine: explicit `--engine` (existence check), then PATH,
   then package-parent `cpp/bloomdex[.exe]` and `build/bloomdex[.exe]`.
   An invalid explicit path ends the search. A missing engine prints an error
   and returns 3; `index` does not fall back to exact scanning.
2. Use `--workdir` or create a temporary directory. Write `ref.norm.txt`
   and `subject.norm.txt`, then `ref.sig` and `subject.sig`.
   There is no cleanup in this command. Reusing a directory overwrites these
   fixed filenames, so use a separate directory per retained run.
3. Sign both corpora with defaults K=128, n=5, minimum token length=1, seed=0.
   The bridge exposes minimum-token and seed parameters, but the Python CLI
   does not. C++ seed 0 selects the fixed internal seed `0xB100D`.
4. Match signatures at default estimated-Jaccard threshold 0.5, writing
   `--out` or `match.tsv` in the work directory. Logs/path messages go to
   stdout; a rate verdict goes to stderr. This path does not emit scan-style JSON.
5. `report FILE` parses TSV and prints flagged-pair count, distinct flagged
   reference IDs and the top 10 overlaps by default. It lacks the original
   reference population and does not compute a contamination rate.

A signature line is `id<TAB>token_count<TAB>K space-separated unsigned hashes`,
with no header. C++ assigns IDs `r0`, `r1`, etc. from zero-based normalized
line positions, skipping empty token lists while still advancing the counter.
Even with `--id-field`, `index` does not preserve original JSON IDs.
Its rate denominator is the count of loaded reference records, including any
that produce no signature.

Match TSV has header `ref_id<TAB>subject_id<TAB>jaccard`; self-match TSV has
`id_a<TAB>id_b<TAB>jaccard`. Self-match defaults to threshold 0.8 and omits
self-pairs and reversed duplicates. The Python parser discards the first line
as a header and accepts subsequent lines with exactly three tab-separated fields;
numeric conversion can raise an error.

MinHash compares the fraction of equal signature positions. Use identical
normalization, n, K, seed, minimum-token rules and engine version on both inputs.
The format records neither those settings nor a format version. Different
signature widths score zero; incompatible same-width signatures are not detected.
Retain settings alongside artifacts. C++ uses deterministic splitmix64 seeds and
modular hashing with an `unsigned __int128` intermediate; compiler support for
that extension matters beyond the C++17 language label.

## Verification gaps and next work

The [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md) remains the feature plan. It does not identify an
active owner, delivery date or selected next feature. The following are
source-review findings and suggested verification work, not approved new scope.

| Finding and consequence | Useful next check in an authorized full checkout |
| --- | --- |
| README/changelog describe CI compile, syntax and smoke checks, but no `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is present in the supplied inventory. No test suite or retained run results were supplied. | Locate or restore the intended workflow; run contributor checks and record actual results before claiming CI or release verification. |
| Exact and C++ paths use different metrics and ID schemes. Default normalization loses non-ASCII content, empty records affect denominators, and duplicate exact IDs overwrite records. | Check these cases explicitly before interpreting an assay; decide separately whether behavior should change. |
| `match --top` is parsed but its branch only discards `best_id`; it emits no extra pair and does not limit results. The comment claiming a below-threshold best match is misleading. | Treat C++ `--top` as ineffective until implemented and tested. Python scan/report `--top` are separate working code paths. |
| C++ numeric arguments lack range checks; malformed numeric strings/signature fields use throwing conversions. | Validate n, K, thresholds and malformed inputs before treating the engine as robust for untrusted corpora. |
| The hash helper is described as FNV-1a, but starts at `1469598103934665603`, not the standard 64-bit offset basis `14695981039346656037`. | Preserve engine compatibility when consuming old signatures; assess any correction as a format/compatibility change rather than assuming standard FNV output. |
| Metadata's homepage and changelog URLs use `example.invalid`. | Confirm canonical public URLs before release; the existing security policy supplies its own reporting route. |

The contribution guide asks for an issue before work larger than a bug fix,
focused changes, and a test for changed behavior. Its documented checks are
`make` and the exact example scan. Build recipes use
`-std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic`; the script prefers clang++ then g++
unless CXX is set. No compiler/platform success was verified here.

The supplied Dependabot configuration specifies weekly pip updates at the
repository root with at most three open pull requests; this is configuration,
not evidence of a running automation service. The supplied ignore file covers
Python build/cache output, C++ binaries, signatures, normalized text,
`match.tsv` and `benchbloom_*/` directories. It contains no rule targeting
these context documents; effective Git ignore/tracking state was not available.

# Examples

Two tiny corpora ship here so you can watch benchbloom flag contamination:

- `benchmark.jsonl` — 5 held-out benchmark items (the "reference").
- `training.jsonl` — 6 training documents (the "subject"). Items `t1`, `t2`,
  and `t5` deliberately paraphrase or copy benchmark items `b2`, `b4`, and `b1`.

## Exact Python scan (no compiler needed)

```bash
python -m benchbloom scan \
  --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \
  --subject examples/training.jsonl \
  --field text --id-field id --ngram 4 --threshold 0.3
```

Pins live in `requirements-dev.txt`; the examples assume the
stock interpreter, no packages required.

Source-derived expectations for this fixture (not a captured run): `b1` in
`t5`, `b2` in `t1`, and `b4` in `t2` each contain the full normalized
reference text and therefore have containment 1.0 with n=4. The expected
summary is 5 reference items, 3 flagged pairs, 3 contaminated reference items,
rate 0.6, peak overlap 1.0, with a HEAVY verdict on stderr. Verify these
expectations in an executable checkout before reporting them as test results.

`--id-field id` is necessary to retain the displayed `b*`/`t*` labels in
the exact scan. Without it, JSONL records receive `j0`, `j1`, etc.

## MinHash engine path (requires the C++ build)

```bash
# 1) build the engine
make            # or: bash cpp/build.sh

# 2) orchestrate normalize -> sign -> match through bloomdex
python -m benchbloom index \
  --ref examples/benchmark.jsonl \
  --subject examples/training.jsonl \
  --field text --k 128 --ngram 4 --threshold 0.4 \
  --out match.tsv

# 3) render the report
python -m benchbloom report match.tsv
```

Compare MinHash estimates to exact **Jaccard**, not the default containment
trigger; use `scan --jaccard-only` with the same n-gram size and threshold.
Larger K generally reduces sampling uncertainty, but no engine run was performed
for this handoff. C++ output uses normalized-line IDs: the intended copied pairs
map to `r0 ↔ r4`, `r1 ↔ r0`, and `r3 ↔ r1`. These mappings identify the
fixture records; they do not assert which approximate scores a run will emit.

## Retained input fixtures

A Markdown-only handoff excludes the original JSONL files. The blocks below
preserve their complete supplied contents. In an authorized executable checkout,
these correspond to the paths used above. Source, compiler and runtime are still
needed; the documentation bundle alone cannot execute the examples.

### benchmark.jsonl

```jsonl

{"id": "b2", "text": "Photosynthesis converts sunlight water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen."}
{"id": "b3", "text": "A prime number greater than two is always odd because two divides all even numbers."}
{"id": "b4", "text": "Xylem transports water upward while phloem distributes sugars throughout the vascular plant."}
{"id": "b5", "text": "The capital of the fictional republic of Verdania is the coastal city of Aloravel."}
```

### training.jsonl

```jsonl

{"id": "t2", "text": "Gardeners know that xylem transports water upward while phloem distributes sugars throughout the vascular plant tissue."}
{"id": "t3", "text": "The chef prepared a wonderful risotto with saffron and aged parmesan on a rainy autumn evening."}
{"id": "t4", "text": "Rockets rely on Newton's third law: every action produces an equal and opposite reaction in the exhaust plume."}
{"id": "t5", "text": "The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the plant cell and drives respiration inside every living tissue."}
{"id": "t6", "text": "A weekly farmers market sells heirloom tomatoes basil and fresh cut sunflowers near the old stone bridge."}
```

See [project context](../docs/context.md) for defaults, ID behavior and known
limitations.
